title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise 2: Within-group(s) statistics — nucleotide diversity
The simplest possible computation we can do is to compute a statistic for a single population. As an example, let’s look at nucleotide diversity (also known as \(\pi\)), implemented by the slendr function ts_diversity().

If you look at its help page under ?ts_diversity, you will see that it accepts several arguments—for now let’s focus on the first two, ts = (which is obviously a tree-sequence object, such as the one produced by the msprime() engine) and sample_sets =.
Compute ts_diversity() on a single simulated individual, such as the individual with the name “pop_1”, by providing this name as the sample_sets = argument of this function. Knowing that slendr simulates diploids and knowing the definition of nucleotide diversity, how would you interpret the result that you get for this one individual from the perspective of genomics?






NoteClick to see the solution





The answer is that we get that individual’s heterozygosity—the proportion of their complete genome (composed of two chromosomes, because each individual is diploid) carrying heterozygous sites:

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = "pop_1")

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 pop_1  0.000207





Note that this is the same thing as the following command:

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1"))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 pop_1  0.000207


This is because in R, a single value is the same thing as a vector of length one (this might seem like a bit of curious R trivia but it’s good to keep in mind):

"single_value" == c("single_value")

[1] TRUE

length(c("single_value"))

[1] 1

length("single_value")

[1] 1






Now run the following three commands, one after the other. They look extremely similar, right? Do they produce the same value? If not, based on the results you get from each of those commands, can you deduce a general rule for how slendr interprets what it gets in the sample_sets = argument?

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_42"))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_42")))



Note: It turns out that patterns like these are very important for computing any kind of tree-sequence statistic with slendr, so it very much pays off to think about this, even though this looks trivial and nitpicky!






NoteClick to see the solution






The first command is supposed to demonstrate that specifying a plain vector of names to a statistic computed within a group computes that statistic as if each individual was “its own group”. In this example, we get individual-based heterozygosity for each of the two individuals separately (notice that the “pop_1” value is the same you got in the previous task):


ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_42"))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  set    diversity
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 pop_1   0.000207
2 pop_42  0.000211



The second command features the same vector of names, but wrapped in list(). This is how you instruct slendr to treat a given set of individuals as a group—and in this case, compute a statistic for the group as a whole. In this context, this command computes the nucleotide diversity within a group formed by the given two individuals from the population “pop”:


ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_42")))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 set_1  0.000206



Notice that in the result above, slendr assigned our group of two individuals a rather non-descriptive group name “set_1”. Because these default names can be confusing in more complex computations of more complex statistics, you can optionally specify the name of your group by providing the set of individuals as a named list instead (see the R bootcamp chapter in case you need a refresher on named lists and similar topics):


# note that the group name "set_1" is now replaced by "pop_subset"
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_42")))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set        diversity
  <chr>          <dbl>
1 pop_subset  0.000206






Of course, we can compute any statistic not only for one group of individuals, but for multiple of them. What result such computation produces depends on whether we’re computing the so-called “one-way statistics” (computed within groups, like nucleotide diversity we started with here) or “multi-way statistics” (computed between groups, like \(F_{ST}\)). For now we’ll stay with one-way statistics.
To make the “one-way” statistic concept clear, let’s practice this. Instead of computing ts_diversity() for a single group of individuals (like “pop_1” and “pop_42” above), compute it on multiple subsets of individuals of increasing samples sizes (let’s say groups of 1, 2, 5, 10, 500 1000, and finally all individuals in the population “pop”). Before you run this computation, do you expect the same value of nucleotide diversity for each of those sample sizes? Why, or why not?
Hint: You can get a random subset of a larger set of elements using the built-in R function sample(). Take a look at ?sample manual page if you need more help. If you need even more help, take a peek at the beginning of the solution below (point 2. specifically). When you have a list of the different subsets of individuals, you can provide it as the sample_sets = argument of ts_diversity() again.






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s first generate the subsets of different sizes. We have a number of options:

We could do it “manually” like this:


# first get all names of all individuals recorded in the tree sequence
# as a single vector stored in the variable named `all`
all <- ts_names(ts)

# then "manually" create all required subsets
subsets <- list(
  sample(all, 1),
  sample(all, 2),
  sample(all, 5),
  sample(all, 10),
  sample(all, 500),
  sample(all, 1000),
  all
)


Alternatively, we could do it more succinctly using this neat R trick:


# first create a vector of the desired sizes of all subsets
sizes <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 500, 1000, length(all))

# then iterate over those sizes, applying the sample() function to each
subsets <- lapply(sizes, sample, x = all)
names(subsets) <- sizes

Either way, both approaches create a list of vectors of appropriate lengths that we need to solve this exercise.

Having created the lists of subsets of individuals from the population, we can finally compute nucleotide diversity in each of those groups like this:

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = subsets)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 1      0.000164
2 2      0.000206
3 5      0.000195
4 10     0.000189
5 500    0.000194
6 1000   0.000194
7 5000   0.000194


Not surprisingly, we don’t see much difference. This is expected, because there is only one true (unknown) value of nucleotide diversity of the entire population. What changes when we compute this statistic on subsets of different sizes is the stochastic noise due to random chance.
We’ll see a bit more on how to control (and quantify) the noise in simulations a little bit later.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise 3: Parameter estimation — \(N_e\)
In practical research, we often use various software to estimate some model parameter of interest. In our context—again, to demonstrate the concept of simulation-based analyses in a familiar context—let’s look at a measure of the population size called effective population size, or \(N_e\), as this model parameter of interest we want to infer.
From a bit of background theory of population genetics, we know that we can obtain an estimate of \(N_e\) from nucleotide diversity (which we just computed). Specifically, neutral theory of molecular evolution posits that an idealised diploid population will have the nucleotide diversity (usually called \(\theta\) in literature) equal to
\[\theta = 4 N_e \mu,\]
where \(\mu\) is the mutation rate. Using simple algebra to rearrange this equation, this gives us an estimate for \(N_e\) which can be computed from nucleotide diversity in the form of
\[N_e = \frac{\theta}{4 \mu}.\]
In principle, this is an estimate which could be computed by some external software (in a more complex real-world scenario). Let’s build a simple simulation-based analysis to determine how well does this estimator perform under different scenarios.


Note: If you are familiar with population genetics, this exercise has all sorts of obvious answers, but let’s demonstrate how we can benchmark this estimate using simulations, establishing a useful slendr recipe which you will be able to use in many other contexts on many other inference methods (some of the more complex ones will be demonstrated later in this workshop).

In your script slendr_statistics.R, start by computing nucleotide diversity across all individuals in your tree sequence taken together (instead of a small subset) and store this result of ts_diversity() in a data frame df. Then, use the equation above to estimate \(N_e\) from nucleotide diversity, adding a new column called Ne_estimated to this data frame with this value. Do you get a somewhat reasonably looking result?
Hint: Remember that you know the true \(N_e\) in your model — it’s the N value in your simulation script! That’s the most powerful thing about simulations — they allow you to establish a ground truth and benchmark various methods against this truth!






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s get the data frame with the value of diversity first:

df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
df

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 all    0.000194


Then add the inferred \(N_e\) according to the equation above:

df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
df

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  set   diversity Ne_estimated
  <chr>     <dbl>        <dbl>
1 all    0.000194        4847.


We programmed the true \(N_e\) in our model at 5000, so this estimate doesn’t look bad at all!



Of course, benchmarking any method based on a single simulation of a single number doesn’t make much sense in practice—so now let’s now take things one step forward.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise 4: Generalizing the simulation
Suppose we need to evaluate how our hypothetical statistic of interest (in this example, our estimator of \(N_e\)) behaves under different parameters, different models, different bioinformatic processing, etc. This happens very often in practical research, so how would we go about it using simulations?
To do this, we could make a copy of our original script, modify it a bunch of times, and re-run the modifications as needed, collecting the results in the process. This works, but is almost always the wrong approach. The correct way to do this is to generalize our code into a self-contained function.
To demonstrate, let’s break this down into individual steps (in software engineering, this process of modifying code and improving it is called “refactoring”).

First, save your current script slendr_statistics.R as a new script called slendr_Ne_pi.R. We’ll be working on improvements in this new file (the pi comes from a shortcut name for nucleotide diversity in mathematical theory \(\pi\)).

In this new script slendr_Ne_pi.R, create a new R function called sim_constant, which will accept a single argument Ne_true, and will “wrap around” the following bits of code (most of which can be copy-pasted from the original slendr_statistics.R you worked on so far in this chapter, with minor modifications):

the code implementing our slendr demographic model (substituting the originally fixed N value for Ne_true, of course),
the command simulating a ts object from the model,
the command creating the df data frame with nucleotide diversity,
the computation of Ne_estimated from nucleotide diversity,
addition of a Ne_true column to df and assigning it the Ne_true argument given to your function.
returning this df object as the output of the function.

When you’re done, all code which was doing the steps above in your original script should be entirely replaced by this function.
Hint: If you need help with creating a custom function, you can use the following template which shows what should your script look like when you’re done. Additionally, you can get a refresher on programming custom functions by skimming the relevant section of the “R bootcamp” chapter.






NoteClick to see the template






library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  # add the bits of code doing steps 1.-5. inside this function

  # finally, return the df data frame like this (step 6.)
  return(df)
}










NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s how my entire slendr_Ne_pi.R looks like. As you can see, it’s basically the same exact code as the script slendr_statistics.R we started with, just “wrapped” in the function(Ne_true) { ... } block.

library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = Ne_true)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}





To test your function, restart your R session (in the RStudio top menu go Session -> Restart R), then run your entire script again. Then, evaluate your function in the R console by running it for different values of \(N_e\) (for instance, type sim_constant(100), sim_constant(1234), sim_constant(20000), etc.). Each of your function calls should produce a data frame with the appropriate value of diversity and the estimated \(N_e\).






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s what I get with my implementation of this function:

sim_constant(Ne_true = 100)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  set    diversity Ne_estimated Ne_true
  <chr>      <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 all   0.00000316         79.1     100

sim_constant(Ne_true = 1234)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  set   diversity Ne_estimated Ne_true
  <chr>     <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 all   0.0000521        1304.    1234

sim_constant(Ne_true = 20000)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  set   diversity Ne_estimated Ne_true
  <chr>     <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 all    0.000801       20037.   20000


Again, it looks like our estimator can—at least on this extremely trivial underlying demographic model—infer the hidden \(N_e\) quite well.




Doing all this extra programming work might seem like unnecessary bother. In fact, it looks like we’ve written even more code to make this happen! But the pay off comes later, I promise.
Custom functions are absolutely critical for efficient, reproducible science. They eliminate copy-pasted bug-prone code and make it much easier to explore ideas, test parameters, and explore various models. In this workshop, I’ll be often forcing you to write custom functions—hopefully, by the end you will appreciate why I did this.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise 5: Simulations across parameter grids
Whenever we want to benchmark a statistic or understand its expected behavior under different circumstances, we need to re-run a model many times, usually for different model parameters (or even different models entirely).
Imagine we want to repeat our inference on many different potential values of true \(N_e\). What we could do is something like what you did while testing your function earlier, running the variations of the simulation individually and manually. But this isn’t scalable, definitely not if we need to run the same model across a huge number of parameter values (or even multiple sets of such parameters).
In cases like this, we can use a “looping” function, such as the very convenient function map_dfr() from the package purrr.

Let’s demonstrate how this technique works. You don’t have to run any of this code, just skim through this demonstration to get an idea how this works and apply it later.
Imagine a silly little function like this, which creates a data frame with a given number and its square:

# define a custom function
silly_fun <- function(x) {
  return(data.frame(value = x, squared = x * x))
}

# run it for the value of x = 10
silly_fun(10)

  value squared
1    10     100


The way you use map_dfr is by providing a list of values of our parameter of interest and a name of some function. In the case of our silly function, we can use map_dfr() like this:

library(purrr)

map_dfr(c(10, 100, 1234, 20000), silly_fun)

  value   squared
1    10       100
2   100     10000
3  1234   1522756
4 20000 400000000


The name map_dfr stands for “map a given function producing a data frame and then bind its rows together”, hence, map_dfr. When you look at its output above, this is exactly what happened.

In your script slendr_Ne_pi.R, use the same technique program an automated simulation of \(N_e\) inference across a grid of Ne_true values of c(1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000). Use the function map_dfr() to do this in an efficient, automated way, thus obtaining a single data frame. Then, visualize the results in this data frame as a scatterplot of columns Ne_true against Ne_estimated. You can use ggplot2, or base-R plotting, whatever you find easier.






NoteClick to see the solution






library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_constant <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_constant)

ggplot(df_constant, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (constant population size)")












This toy exercise is a great example of how to use these kinds of simulations in practice. Again, nucleotide diverisity-based \(N_e\) estimation and its benchmarking across a range of parameters is only an example for demonstration, but this idea extends to many other settings:

benchmarking of IBD accuracy across different gene-flow scenarios,
validating qpAdm inference results for various possible admixture graphs,
testing the robustness of local ancestry inference methods (LAI) and admixture dating inference as a function of admixture times and proportions,
understanding how PCA differs for different sample sizes from different populations,

… and many others.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise 6: Comparing multiple models
Let’s make it a bit more interesting and more practically relevant. Suppose we want to see how robust our estimator is to the assumptions behind the underlying demographic model (which is almost always uncertain to some degree, meaning that our assumptions can be also uncertain!).
In the previous exercise, we used nucleotide diversity to infer the \(N_e\) of a population under study (we used an equation, but it could be also external software) and verified that it works very well for a model of a constant population size.
But what about population that experienced a resize event? How well does our \(N_e\) estimate work in such case?

In your script slendr_Ne_pi.R, make a copy of your function sim_constant() and name that copy sim_change(). Make the following changes to this function:

the population “pop” will start with fixed \(N_e\) of 5000,
the population will experience a population resize (implemented by the function resize()), which will set the size of the population to the value given to the argument Ne_true at time 1000.

Then, use map_dfr() to run the new function sim_change() along the same parameter grid as before, visualizing the results of Ne_true against Ne_estimated again. How well does our diversity-based \(N_e\) estimate perform in such a demographic scenario? Is it robust to non-constant demographic histories? If not, why?






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the solution—new function sim_change(), new simulation run against a parameter grid, and a visualization of results:

# new function to simulate population size change
sim_change <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <-
    population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>%
    resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# simulations across a parameter grid
Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_change <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change)

# visualization of results
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000)

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









We can see that even a large population resize event doesn’t change the observed levels of nucleotide diversity that much. As a result, the \(N_e\) based on the population nucleotide diversity is very wrong—we consistently estimate it at the level of 5000 (i.e., the size prior to the resize), regardless of the true size of the population after the resize.
It’s only very drastic bottlenecks that are picked up by our \(N_e\) estimator, and even in those cases we still severely overestimate the true \(N_e\) after the resize event.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise 7: Expanding the parameter grid
Our hypothesis for how poorly the nucleotide diversity-based estimate of \(N_e\) is doing under non-constant population size is that the resize event is very recent. As a result, diversity hasn’t yet reached an equilibrium value which would be picked up by our \(N_e\) estimator.
Let’s test this hypothesis while, at the same time, showing how we can expand the parameter grid simulations to include another parameter—this time the time of the population size change in addition to the \(N_e\) resize value.

In your script slendr_Ne_pi.R, add a second argument to your function sim_change() called T_change. Change the resize() command in your function to use variable T_change instead of the fixed value of 1000, then add another column called T_change to the data frame with the value of this argument before the function returns the results again. Then, run four versions of the map_dfr() command in the same way as before, except now in the form such as map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 100) (this will run sim_change() for each of the Ne_grid values like before, while fixing the T_change parameter to 100). Do this for T_change of 1, 100, 1000, and 2000.
When you visualize the results for each of the four simulation batches, do you see evidence supporting our hypothesis for why our \(N_e\) estimator performs poorly in sudden changes of \(N_e\)? And does the time since the resize change have an effect on the estimator as we hypothesized?






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the solution.
First, the new function sim_change() which now has two parameters Ne_true and T_change:

sim_change <- function(Ne_true, T_change) {
  pop <-
    population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>%
    resize(N = Ne_true, time = T_change)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  df$T_change <- T_change
  
  df
}

A new simulation run against a parameter grid (I’m rbind()-ing all four map_dfr() runs together because I want to use ggplot2 to visualize the results in a tidy way with four panels:

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_change <- rbind(
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 1),    # simulate size change 1 generation ago
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 100),  # simulate size change 100 generations ago
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 1000), # etc.
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 2000)
)

And finally, visualization of results:

ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)",
          subtitle = "Each panel indicates the time of the population size change") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000) +
  facet_wrap(~ T_change)

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









Here’s the same result, plotted in a single figure:

library(dplyr)

df_change %>%
  mutate(T_change = factor(T_change)) %>% 
ggplot(aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated, color = T_change, group = T_change)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000)








We can see that, indeed, the older the population resize event, the more time there’s for the population to lose genetic variation (in case of a bottleneck), or gain new variation (in case of population size increase—though we don’t really see the effect here), which means that the \(N_e\) estimated based on the \(\theta = 4 N_e \mu\) nucleotide diversity parameter is going to be a little closer to the true (unknown) population size.
Still, it’s absolutely clear that non-constant demography can completely mislead the \(N_e\) estimator based on nucleotide diversity—this is a conclusion that is actually quite relevant for real-world applications. For instance, we could have very endangered species (with a very small \(N_e\)) which still maintains quite a bit of nucleotide diversity!




In conclusion, the problem with the nucleotide diversity is that it effectively reduces the entirety of genetic variation in the population (which mutations there are at which frequencies) into a single number. As a result, we lose a lot of potentially very useful information about the population’s demographic history. When we try to estimate \(N_e\) using this summary statistic, we can only hope to infer a long-term \(N_e\), but we won’t be able to infer recent population dynamics.
As we have seen, a single bottleneck doesn’t cause nucleotide diversity to drop significantly enough for us to pick up that this bottleneck even happened.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise 8: Real-world example
To put the simulation-based exploration above in a real-world context, let’s consider the case of estimating the \(N_e\) of a present-day modern human population.
Take a look at the Supplementary Table 1 published in this hugely influential paper. Look up the value of heterozygosity computed for the individual with the sample ID “S_Czech-2” in the column called “samtools autosomal heterozygosity”. What is the \(N_e\) value you can estimate from the heterozygosity observed in this individual, if you assume autosomal human mutation rate \(\mu\) of \(1.3 × 10^{−8}\) per base pair, per generation (1.3e-8 in R) and substitute the individual’s heterozygosity for the \(\theta\) parameter?
Knowing what you’ve learned from your simulation benchmarking of this simple \(N_e\) estimator above, how does your inferred modern human \(N_e\) fit in the context of the fact that there are more than 8 billion people in the world right now?






NoteClick to see the solution





In the Excel sheet we see the following heterozygosity for this individual:

theta <- 0.00085124

Using our \(N_e\) equation, this gives us the estimate of \(N_e\) like this:

Ne <- theta / (4 * 1.3e-8)
Ne

[1] 16370


We can see that this \(N_e\) value is drastically lower compared to the billions of people alive today. This reflects the fact that—although there are so many of us alive today—human population for most of our history was very small, which is why the \(N_e\) that we estimated reflects a kind of average of population sizes over the past few millions of years.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Bonus exercise: Allele frequency spectrum (AFS)
Create a new script called slendr_Ne_afs.R. Copy-paste the following code into that script. Note that this is the same exact model we started this chapter with (except for the one line which selects only 20 individuals from all individuals recorded in the tree sequence).

library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000)
model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)


Unlike nucleotide diversity which, as mentioned above, reduces the entire genomic variation of a population into a single number, the allele frequency spectrum carries information about the distribution of the counts of mutations at each observable frequency.
Look at the ?ts_afs help page to learn how the slendr function ts_afs() works. As you’ve seen, ts_diversity() (like the vast majority of slendr statistical functions) produces a data frame. What data format does ts_afs() produce? Compute the AFS from your simulated tree sequence ts on your subset of individuals, then visualize it (with whatever means you know).






NoteClick to see the solution





As we can see, ts_afs() produces a plain R vector of integer numbers, each of which represents the count of mutations observed at a given frequency — the count of singletons, the count of doubletons, etc.:

afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
afs

 [1] 12459  1888  1055   749   463   422   382   302   255   233   181   169
[13]   139   130   167   126   117    93   106    96   112


This vector can be easily visualized with a base-R function plot():

plot(afs, type = "l", col = "lightblue", xlab = "allele frequency", ylab = "count")












But does the AFS really carry more information about demographic changes?
Write a new function in your script, called sim_afs(), which will again accept a single argument Ne_true and implement the exact same demographic model as you did in your function sim_change() (i.e., resize from the initial N of 5000 to the given value of Ne_true at time 1000). In this function, compute the afs vector from this model, then run it for a range of Ne_grid values and visualize the individual AFS vectors produced for each of them. Does AFS pick up signal even from such recent population size changes, unlike the nucleotide diversity?






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s a function which simulates an AFS for a demographic history given by the Ne_true argument:

library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_afs <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)

  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  # return the result not as a plain integer vector, but a proper data frame
  # annotated by the frequency bin number -- this makes visualization of
  # results later with ggplot2 much easier
  data.frame(
    Ne_true = Ne_true,
    frequency = 1:length(afs),
    count = afs
  )
}

We run the AFS simulation batch in the same way as we did before:

df_afs <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_afs)

And we visualize the individual AFS vectors, colored by their underlying assumed \(N_e\) after the demographic history change:

ggplot(df_afs, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
  geom_line() +
  ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models")








For easier comparison, here are the AFS result side-by-side with the values of nucleotide diversity from the same demographic scenarios:


`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









This simulation indicates that AFS does, indeed, carry much more information about population history, even for recent changes in population size, driven largely by singletons! Therefore, at least for population expansions, AFS is much more statistically powerful than nucleotide diversity. From population genetic theory perspective this makes sense, because nucleotide diversity is actually nothing but a summary of the AFS.




For now we’ll leave this topic be. We could go much deeper into this, but the point of this chapter was to demonstrate how to compute within-population statistics with slendr, how we can use manipulation of R lists and vectors to instruct slendr on how to compute a given statistic, and provide a set of small examples of how population genomic simulations (even extremely simple ones!) and a bit of data processing can be used to benchmark real-world inference methods..
Towards the end of the workshop, you’ll have the opportunity work through a slightly more realistic case-study which will demonstrate how to do simulation-based inference of \(N_e\) in a fully automated way.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Catching up
Here is a complete solution to the exercises in this section represented by a single tidy reproducible R script:






NoteClick to see the entire script





For simplicity, this script only evaluates models when the size change happens 1000 generations ago (but it could be expanded, of course).

# first we import a couple of packages ------------------------------------

library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

library(slendr)
init_env()

# function which simulates a constant size model --------------------------

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = Ne_true)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
  
  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
  
  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# function which simulates a model of population size change --------------

sim_change <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
  
  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
  
  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# function which simulates the AFS from a size change model ---------------

sim_afs <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  # return the result not as a plain integer vector, but a proper data frame
  # annotated by the frequency bin number
  data.frame(
    Ne_true = Ne_true,
    frequency = 1:length(afs),
    count = afs
  )
}

# run simulations across a given grid -------------------------------------

# for the constant model, these values represent the constant Ne, for the size
# change model they represent the final Ne after the initial size of 5000

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_constant <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_constant)
df_change <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change)
df_afs <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_afs)

# visualize the results ---------------------------------------------------

# diversity in the constant size models
ggplot(df_constant, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (constant population size)")

ggsave("constant_size_pi.pdf")

# diversity in the size change models
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000)

ggsave("changing_size_pi.pdf")

# AFS in the size change models
ggplot(df_afs, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
  geom_line() +
  ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models")

ggsave("changing_size_afs.pdf")

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Theme of this chapter
In this chapter, we will move from computing “within-group” population genetic statistics to “between-group” statistics. In a couple of practical exercises, we will implement “recipes” showcasing how simulation-based exploration allows us to characterize the expected behavior of statistics of interest under various relevant demographic scenarios to confidently understand their strengths and limitations. In the process, we will (re-)discover a couple of known features of \(F_{ST}\) and \(f_3\) statistics highly relevant for practical research.

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Literature

Chapter 2.4, “2.4 Genetic drift in structured populations.”: As mentioned in the introduction, to do the exercises in this chapter, you don’t have to know more about \(F_{ST}\) other than that it’s a frequently useful metric of genetic differentiation between two populations scaled between 0 (no differentiation, i.e. both groups form a single panmictic population) to 1 (complete differentiation without any shared genetic variation betweeen the two groups). Still, if you want to know a bit more about the technical details (and many, many caveats) of \(F_{ST}\), take a look at the linked chapter of the book “An Owner’s Guide to the Human Genome”, specifically section titled “Measuring population structure: FST”.
If you want to know much more technical background into \(f_3\) statistics (introduced in this chapter), and \(f_4\) statistics and admixture proportion estimators \(f_4\)-ratio (introduced in the following chapter), you can take a look at the following papers: Peter, 2016, Lipson 2020, and Patterson et al., 2012.

title: Between-population statistics
section: Exercise 1: Recap on working with R lists and nested vectors
text:
Exercise 1: Recap on working with R lists and nested vectors
In the previous chapter, you learned to compute within-group summary statistics which is done by providing single vectors of individual names (most easily obtained by the function ts_names()) to various slendr functions in a very straightforward way.
Whenever we work with “between-group statistics” (statistics based on comparisons of genomic variation between different groups of individuals, also known as “multi-way statistics”in tskit which slendr uses as an internal statistical computation engine), we need to be aware of a couple of things with regards to how R handles nested lists of vectors.
Let’s first set up a small model to demonstrate this concept again and to practice it in an easy-to-understand context.

Start by creating a new R script called split_simulation.R and program the three-population model (populations called “outgroup”, “X”, and “Y”) in the following sketch in this script. Simulate a tree sequence object ts (sequence length 10Mb, recombination rate 1e-8, mutation rate 1e-8) from this model, scheduling the recording of ten individuals from each of the three populations at time 0 (i.e., the “present-day”).



Hint: As a gentle reminder, unlike our previous toy examples, this model features multiple populations, so you will need to program population splits. Remember that you can specify that a population should split from some parent lineage by using the population(..., parent = <parent population>) format.






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s what’s in my split_simulation.R script:

library(slendr)
init_env()

outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 1000, time = 10000)
X <- population("X", N = 1000, time = 3000, parent = outgroup)
Y <- population("Y", N = 1000, time = 3000, parent = outgroup)

model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, X, Y), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

plot_model(model, order = c("outgroup", "X", "Y"), proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule)








ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)





Let’s do a recap of a couple of vector- and list-based operations in R, which are used in slendr all the time (you can refresh your memory on this topic by scrolling through the introductory R bootcamp chapter, particularly sections about subsetting and indexing into vectors and lists).
You’re already familiar with calling the function ts_names() as ts_names(ts) and know that it produces a plain vector of individual names. Now, add the following line to your script:

samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

When you type samples in your R console, What is the type of the data stored in it? What does this information tell us and how is it different from running simply ts_names(ts)?






NoteClick to see the solution






The command ts_names(ts) produces a vector of all individuals recorded in the tree sequence, as we can see here:


samples <- ts_names(ts)
# samples is a "character vector"
class(samples)

[1] "character"

samples

 [1] "X_1"         "X_2"         "X_3"         "X_4"         "X_5"        
 [6] "X_6"         "X_7"         "X_8"         "X_9"         "X_10"       
[11] "Y_1"         "Y_2"         "Y_3"         "Y_4"         "Y_5"        
[16] "Y_6"         "Y_7"         "Y_8"         "Y_9"         "Y_10"       
[21] "outgroup_1"  "outgroup_2"  "outgroup_3"  "outgroup_4"  "outgroup_5" 
[26] "outgroup_6"  "outgroup_7"  "outgroup_8"  "outgroup_9"  "outgroup_10"



The variation ts_names(ts, split = TRUE) gives us a (named! this is important!) list of vectors, one for each population.


samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
# samples is a list
class(samples)

[1] "list"

samples

$outgroup
 [1] "outgroup_1"  "outgroup_2"  "outgroup_3"  "outgroup_4"  "outgroup_5" 
 [6] "outgroup_6"  "outgroup_7"  "outgroup_8"  "outgroup_9"  "outgroup_10"

$X
 [1] "X_1"  "X_2"  "X_3"  "X_4"  "X_5"  "X_6"  "X_7"  "X_8"  "X_9"  "X_10"

$Y
 [1] "Y_1"  "Y_2"  "Y_3"  "Y_4"  "Y_5"  "Y_6"  "Y_7"  "Y_8"  "Y_9"  "Y_10"






Using operations for indexing and subsetting of R lists, how would you access the names of individuals in the population X? Specifically, what’s the difference between calling samples$X, samples[["X"]], and samples["X"]? Try to answer first without running these commands, then run them in the R console to verify your intuition.






NoteClick to see the solution






The first command extracts a “standalone” vector of X individuals from the list:


samples$X

 [1] "X_1"  "X_2"  "X_3"  "X_4"  "X_5"  "X_6"  "X_7"  "X_8"  "X_9"  "X_10"

length(samples$X)

[1] 10



The same goes for the second variant:


samples[["X"]]

 [1] "X_1"  "X_2"  "X_3"  "X_4"  "X_5"  "X_6"  "X_7"  "X_8"  "X_9"  "X_10"

length(samples[["X"]])

[1] 10



The third command is very different. It looks the same, superficially, but it’s actually a list with a single element (the vector of names)!


samples["X"]

$X
 [1] "X_1"  "X_2"  "X_3"  "X_4"  "X_5"  "X_6"  "X_7"  "X_8"  "X_9"  "X_10"

length(samples["X"])

[1] 1






Why does any of this matter?
Remember how in the previous chapter, you needed to specify a subset of individuals in a slightly convoluted way in order to compute a statistic on them, such as:

list(group_name = c("X_1", "X_2", "X_3"))

$group_name
[1] "X_1" "X_2" "X_3"


Doing so for complex computations is very annoying. But also—notice how the following command produces the same format of data as the above:

samples["X"]

$X
 [1] "X_1"  "X_2"  "X_3"  "X_4"  "X_5"  "X_6"  "X_7"  "X_8"  "X_9"  "X_10"


This is why I implemented the variant ts_names(ts, split = TRUE) in slendr, as a shortcut for not having to deal with named lists of vectors. This makes it possible to use the samples variable to instruct slendr to perform more complex multi-population calculations very efficiently.

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Exercise 2: “Outgroup” \(f_3\) statistic
The \(f_3\) statistic is a famous population genetic metric formally established by Nick Patterson and David Reich in 2008. In practice, the statistic is used in two formulations:

as a measure of shared drift between two populations (also known as the “outgroup” \(f_3\) formulation), or
as an admixture test (also known as the “admixture \(f_3\)” formulation, something we’ll look at later).

As the name implies, \(f_3\) statistic involves the specification of three different lineages (usually populations, or groups of samples from those populations) often called A, B, and C in various mathematical equations, making it a good starting example of how to compute multi-population statistics in slendr
Let’s develop a simulation-based model which will allow us to explore some practically relevant features of this important summary statistic.

Let’s start by doing a couple of modifications to our script split_simulation.R:

Wrap the code in a function called simulate_split() and update it so that this function accepts a single argument tsplit and uses it to specify the point at the “X” and “Y” populations split from the “outgroup” lineage (instead of having a fixed value for the split time as you have now).
Add the computation of the outgroup \(f_3\) statistic, using the function ts_f3(), setting the “X” individuals as the B = argument, “Y” individuals as the C = argument, and the A = argument to the “outgroup” individuals (remember to use the samples variable produced by ts_names() to do this).
The function should return a data frame produced by the ts_f3() function, with a new column named tsplit containing the value of this function argument.

As you see, this is similar to what we did in the previous chapter and over time, you will recognize this as common pattern in simulation-based inference and computer programming in general.


Note: The \(f_3\) statistic is traditionally expressed as \(f_3(A, B; C)\), where C represents the outgroup. Unfortunately, in tskit the outgroup is named A, with B and C being the pair of samples from which we trace the length of branches towards the outgroup, so the statistic is interpreted as \(f_3(B, C;
A).\)






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the content of the script split_simulation.R:

library(slendr)
init_env()

simulate_split <- function(tsplit) {
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 1000, time = 10000)
  X <- population("X", N = 1000, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  Y <- population("Y", N = 1000, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, X, Y), generation_time = 1)
  
  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  
  df <- ts_f3(ts, A = samples["outgroup"], B = samples["X"], C = samples["Y"])
  df$tsplit <- tsplit
  
  return(df)
}





Test your function simulate_split() by calling it on a few split time values in your R console. When you’re confident that you programmed the function correctly, use the familiar function map_dfr() from the purrr package to run simulations of split times between 1 and 10000 generations in steps of every 1000 generations (see ?seq for a reminder on how to do this). Visualize the statistical expectation of the \(f_3\) statistic in a scatterplot as a function of the split time. Add all this analysis code in your script split_simulation.R after your function definition, so that you have it properly recorded as a reproducible pipeline.






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s test the function first:

simulate_split(tsplit = 1000)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  A        B     C     statistic               f3 tsplit
  <chr>    <chr> <chr> <chr>                <dbl>  <dbl>
1 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000125   1000

simulate_split(tsplit = 2000)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  A        B     C     statistic               f3 tsplit
  <chr>    <chr> <chr> <chr>                <dbl>  <dbl>
1 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000190   2000

simulate_split(tsplit = 5000)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  A        B     C     statistic               f3 tsplit
  <chr>    <chr> <chr> <chr>                <dbl>  <dbl>
1 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000501   5000


Now we can run it on a grid of parameter values:

library(purrr)
f3_outgroup <- map_dfr(seq(1, 10000, by = 1000), simulate_split)

We can verify that we did, indeed, get a tidy table of the expected \(f_3\) values for a range of possible split times by typing the result into the R console:

f3_outgroup

# A tibble: 10 × 6
   A        B     C     statistic                 f3 tsplit
   <chr>    <chr> <chr> <chr>                  <dbl>  <dbl>
 1 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.000000237      1
 2 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.00000927    1001
 3 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000210     2001
 4 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000283     3001
 5 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000433     4001
 6 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000520     5001
 7 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000579     6001
 8 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000676     7001
 9 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000779     8001
10 outgroup X     Y     f3(outgroup;X,Y) 0.0000916     9001


And we can finally visualize our results:

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(f3_outgroup, aes(tsplit, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10000)) +
  ggtitle("Expected f3 value as a function of split time") +
  xlab("Split time [generations ago]")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









We can see that, as expected, the \(f_3\) statistic gives a nearly zero for the model involving an extremely recent split of X and Y populations from the outgroup lineage. As you’ll see later, this is consistent with mathematical theory which defined \(f_3\) as the length of the shared branch of X and Y towards the outgroup sample which is, in this case, almost nonexistent (only 1 generation long). To demonstrate this by visualizing such a model (which, necessarily, looks a bit silly):









On the other hand, the older the split time from the outgroup, the longer the shared branch is. Again, to demonstrate the “shared branch length” graphically on a model with the split time of 9001 generations ago:












With this initial setup out of the way, let’s delve into using our small simulation pipeline to answer a couple of practically relevant questions.

title: Between-population statistics
section: Exercise 3: Statistical power of \(F_{ST}\) vs outgroup \(f_3\)
text:
Exercise 3: Statistical power of \(F_{ST}\) vs outgroup \(f_3\)
Another statistic which is very frequently used as a measure of population differentiation is \(F_{ST}\). Let’s say we want to understand which of the two statistics (\(f_3\) or \(F_{ST}\)) is more robust to \(N_e\) differences between the two populations under study.
Recall that \(N_e\) determines the amount of genetic drift (and, therefore, the rate of the loss of genomic variation) in a population. In other words, if you were interested in measuring how far in the past two populations began differentiating, would both of them give you a reliable answer, regardless of the \(N_e\) of those populations under study?
Both \(F_{ST}\) and \(f_3\) are routinely used as measures of population differentiation—can we use them equivalently? Does one have potentially more statistical power than the other? They are sometimes used quite interchangeably in practical research—could it sometimes be a problem?

We want to evaluate the impact of \(N_e\), so let’s modify our function simulate_split() a little bit first:

Right now the function accepts a single argument tsplit. Add a second argument to this function called Ne, then modify the two lines of code programming the splits of X and Y populations from the outgroup and change the fixed values of N = 1000 to use the new flexible parameters Ne.
Modify the function so that it returns in the resulting data frame not only containing the \(f_3\) value (computed by ts_f3()) but also the \(F_{ST}\) value (computed by ts_fst()). You can look up the help in ?ts_fst to see how to use this function.
The data frame returned by the function should now include not only the tsplit column (containing the value of the tsplit argument) as well as the column Ne (containing the value of the Ne argument).

Finally, run the code for the function in your R console, then test it on a couple of tsplit and Ne parameter values.






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s how the modified function looks like. Hopefully this is starting to look like a routine for you (because this is where we eventually want to get):

simulate_split <- function(tsplit, Ne) {
  # create a generalized demographic model
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 1000, time = 10000)
  X <- population("X", N = Ne, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  Y <- population("Y", N = Ne, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, X, Y), generation_time = 1)
  
  # program recording of individuals from each model and simulate their
  # genomic sequences
  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))
  ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # compute Fst and f3 statistics
  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  value_fst <- ts_fst(ts, sample_sets = samples[c("X", "Y")])$Fst
  value_f3 <- ts_f3(ts, A = samples["outgroup"], B = samples["X"], C = samples["Y"])$f3

  # compose the resulting data frame
  df <- data.frame(statistic = c("Fst", "f3"), value = c(value_fst, value_f3))
  df$tsplit <- tsplit
  df$Ne <- Ne
  
  return(df)
}

And here’s how we can check that the function works:

simulate_split(tsplit = 3000, Ne = 100)

  statistic        value tsplit  Ne
1       Fst 9.293336e-01   3000 100
2        f3 2.821368e-05   3000 100

simulate_split(tsplit = 3000, Ne = 1000)

  statistic        value tsplit   Ne
1       Fst 4.207221e-01   3000 1000
2        f3 2.639768e-05   3000 1000

simulate_split(tsplit = 3000, Ne = 5000)

  statistic        value tsplit   Ne
1       Fst 1.068754e-01   3000 5000
2        f3 2.644437e-05   3000 5000






Now that you have your updated function tested, use it to program a new batch of parameter grid simulations into your script pipeline using the looping function map_dfr(), this time fixing tsplit = 3000 and simulating the model for the values of the \(N_e\) parameter. You can use the following code:

# define values of the Ne parameter grid
Ne_grid <- c(100, seq(from = 1000, to = 10000, by = 1000))

# note that although our new function requires two arguments (Ne and tsplit),
# we can loop over one parameter (Ne), while fixing the other (tsplit)
df_tsplit3k <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, simulate_split, tsplit = 3000)

When you’re done, visualize the expected values of f3 and Fst summary statistics as functions of \(N_e\) (and, therefore, as a function of the amount of genetic drift).






NoteClick to see the solution






ggplot(df_tsplit3k, aes(Ne, value, color = statistic)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("Fst and f3 for X-Y split at 3000 generations ago, assuming given Ne")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









Conclusion: the \(f_3\) statistic really is an unbiased estimator of population divergence with respect to \(N_e\) of the two lineages. On the other hand, \(F_{ST}\) is not a great metric of a population split, even though it’s sometimes colloquially used in this phylogenetic sense.
However, to be fair, this is not surprising, because \(F_{ST}\) measures population differentiation! If the \(N_e\) is huge, both X and Y lineages can retain most of the genomic variation which arose in their ancestor (unless they diverged a very long time ago). On the other hand, \(f_3\) truly measures the shared branch length which is, by definition, accurately indicative of the population divergence.




Now, program a second batch of the same grid simulations in your script below the last batch, this time fixing tsplit to 9999 generations ago. What changes when you visualize these new results in the same way as above, with regards to the patterns shown by \(f_3\) and \(F_{ST}\)?






NoteClick to see the solution





We only need to rerun the simulation loop and visualise the results:

df_tsplit10k <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, simulate_split, tsplit = 9999)

Here’s a visualization of the new results:

ggplot(df_tsplit10k, aes(Ne, value, color = statistic)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("Fst and f3 for X-Y split at 9999 generations ago, assuming given Ne")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









When we compare both results side-by-side, we see the difference right away. The split time at 3000 generations ago meant that, when the populations have large \(N_e\), they retain lots of shared genetic variation, leading to a very low \(F_{ST}\) (actually, consistent with zero) which indicates they are not differentiated (upper row). However, the older the split time between the two populations, the more genetic drift causes both “X” and “Y” to become differentiated which is manifested by a higher \(F_{ST}\) value even for very high \(N_e\):


`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'
`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









Crucially, however, note that \(f_3\) is completely robust to the amount of genetic drift (i.e., the \(N_e\) of the populations in question)—it always measures the correct branch length, regardless of the \(N_e\) in the assumed model.

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Catching up
Here is a complete solution to the exercises so far, represented by a single reproducible R script split_simulation.R.






NoteClick to see the script split_simulation.R






library(slendr)
init_env()

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

# this is the second version of the function simulate_split() which accepts
# both tsplit and Ne as function arguments
simulate_split <- function(tsplit, Ne) {
  # set up the three-population demographic model
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 1000, time = 10000)
  X <- population("X", N = Ne, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  Y <- population("Y", N = Ne, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, X, Y), generation_time = 1)
  
  # simulate a tree sequence which will record a defined set of 25 individuals
  # from each population at the end of the simulation (i.e., "present-day")
  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 25))
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # extract the list of names of individuals in each population for convenience
  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  
  # compute both summary statistics and extract their values as single numbers
  value_fst <- ts_fst(ts, sample_sets = samples[c("X", "Y")])$Fst
  value_f3 <- ts_f3(ts, A = samples["outgroup"], B = samples["X"], C = samples["Y"])$f3

  # construct a data frame with all the necessary information
  df <- data.frame(statistic = c("Fst", "f3"), value = c(value_fst, value_f3))
  df$tsplit <- tsplit
  df$Ne <- Ne
  
  return(df)
}


# this is the original exploration of f3 as a function of split time, slightly
# tweaked to use the version of simulate_split() parametrizable by both
# tsplit and Ne (recall that the first version used only the tsplit argument)
f3_outgroup <- map_dfr(seq(1, 10000, by = 1000), simulate_split, Ne = 1000)

# and visualization of the results
f3_outgroup %>%
filter(statistic == "f3", Ne == 1000) %>%
ggplot(aes(tsplit, value)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10000))


# this is the comparison of the statistical power of Fst and f3 statistics with
# respect to the amount of genetic drift in both lineages
Ne_grid <- c(100, seq(from = 1000, to = 10000, by = 1000))
f3_vs_fst <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, simulate_split, tsplit = 3000)

# and visualization of the f3-vs-Fst comparison
ggplot(f3_vs_fst, aes(Ne, value, color = statistic)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("Fst and f3 for X-Y split at 3000 generations ago, assuming given Ne")

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Exercise 4: “Admixture” \(f_3\)
Now let’s explore the application of \(f_3\) statistic in its other common use, which is an admixture test. Our primary interest in this exercise will be to investigate the limits of \(f_3\) to detect evidence of admixture—in particular, if we see a “non-significant” \(f_3\) statistic (“admixture \(f_3\)” is considered statistically not significant when it has a positive value), which factors could make this test being a false negative?
To do this, we will need to expand our baseline population model a little bit.

Create a new script, this time calling it admixture_simulation.R. Paste the following skeleton of a model into this script, read it and try to decipher what kind of model does it program (it’s obvious from the text above, but still, do this as another code-reading practice). In particular, pay attention to how the admixture is programmed—how does the model encode the formation of the population mix? Run the code and take a look at the plot visualization produced.

library(slendr)
init_env()

library(dplyr)   # manipulating tabular data
library(ggplot2) # data visualization
library(purrr)   # convenient looping functions

# model parameter (currently fixed to these values)
tmix <- 2000 # admixture time
prop <- 0.1  # admixture proportion
Ne <- 5000   # Ne of the admixed population

outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 5000, time = 10000)
x <- population("x", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)
y <- population("y", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)

# this is how we program "mix" as a merge of "x" and "y" populations
mix <- population("mix", N = Ne, time = tmix + 1, parent = x)
gf <- gene_flow(from = y, to = mix, start = tmix, end = tmix - 1, proportion = prop)

model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, x, y, mix), gene_flow = gf, generation_time = 1)

plot_model(model, order = c("outgroup", "x", "mix", "y"), proportions = TRUE)







NoteClick to see the solution





In our model, the x and y populations merge at a time tmix to form a population mix. Note that due to the way in which slendr currently implements population merges, we first need to program the split of the population mix from its parent x at time tmix - 1, followed at time tmix (i.e., immediately in the following generation) by admixture from y at some defined proportion proportion (a value between 0 and 1). To approximate the idea of a population merge as closely as possible within the constraints of the slendr interface, we program this admixture event so that it ends after a single generation (i.e., it should end at time tmix + 1).

plot_model(model, order = c("outgroup", "x", "mix", "y"), proportions = TRUE)








This is a bit of an annoying peculiarity of slendr that I never got to make easier, sorry about that! Maybe one day I will implement population merges as truly “single-generation events”.




Now, we want to establish the limits of statistical power of \(f_3\) to detect signs of admixture across all sorts of parameters, given our general model of interest—and you know what that means! This annoying “refactoring” again…
Transform the admixture_simulation.R script (which has currently fixed values of all demographic parameters) into a generalized function model by wrapping it in a function called simulate_admixture(). For this exercise, your function should accept three arguments:

tmix specifying the time of admixture,
prop specifying the admixture proportion,
Ne specifying the N size of the population mix.

In your function, schedule the recording of 20 individuals from populations x, y, and mix at time 0 (i.e., at the end of the simulation), and program it to simulate a 25 Mb of tree sequence (recombination rate 1e-8, mutation rate 1e-8). Finally, compute the “admixture \(f_3\)” statistic in the appropriate A, B, C configuration, adding the arguments tmix, prop, and Ne to the data frame produced by the ts_f3() function.
Your function will return this data frame as its output. Again, test it on a couple of parameter combinations to make sure it produces results in the desirable format described above.






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s our expanded function:

simulate_admixture <- function(tmix, prop, Ne) {
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 5000, time = 10000)
  x <- population("x", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)
  y <- population("y", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)

  # in this generalized model, admixture parameters for the mixed
  # population are parametrized as tmix, prop, and Ne
  mix <- population("mix", N = Ne, time = tmix + 1, parent = x)
  gf <- gene_flow(from = y, to = mix, start = tmix, end = tmix - 1, proportion = prop)
  
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, x, y, mix), gene_flow = gf, generation_time = 1)

  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(x, 20), list(y, 20), list(mix, 20))

  ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 25e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>% ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  ts_f3(ts, A = samples["mix"], B = samples["x"], C = samples["y"]) %>%
    mutate(tmix = tmix, prop = prop, Ne = Ne)
}

Let’s test it on couple of parameter combinations:

simulate_admixture(tmix = 2000, prop = 0.2, Ne = 10000)

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  A     B     C     statistic           f3  tmix  prop    Ne
  <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>            <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) 0.00000445  2000   0.2 10000

simulate_admixture(tmix = 1000, prop = 0.1, Ne = 10000)

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  A     B     C     statistic            f3  tmix  prop    Ne
  <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>             <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.00000170  1000   0.1 10000

simulate_admixture(tmix = 1,    prop = 0,   Ne = 3000)

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  A     B     C     statistic            f3  tmix  prop    Ne
  <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>             <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) 0.000000216     1     0  3000






Having tested the function on a couple of individual simulations, run it along the range of potential tmix values like this using map_dfr() again, while fixing the admixture proportion to 20% (prop = 0.2) and \(N_e\) to 5000 (Ne = 5000):
Do you see any interesting pattern in the behavior of the admixture \(f_3\) test when you visualize \(f_3\) as a function of the admixture time? Can we rely on it to detect admixture in all scenarios, or does it lose statistical power in some circumstances? Remember, you know that all your simulations have admixture and \(f_3\) detects that admixture only if it has a negative value.






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s run a new grid simulation of our admixture \(f_3\) model:

tmix_grid <- seq(1, 1500, by = 100)

f3_tmix <- map_dfr(tmix_grid, simulate_admixture, prop = 0.2, Ne = 5000)
f3_tmix

# A tibble: 15 × 8
   A     B     C     statistic            f3  tmix  prop    Ne
   <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>             <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.0000129      1   0.2  5000
 2 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.0000142    101   0.2  5000
 3 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.0000138    201   0.2  5000
 4 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.00000672   301   0.2  5000
 5 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.0000109    401   0.2  5000
 6 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.00000801   501   0.2  5000
 7 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.00000715   601   0.2  5000
 8 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.00000428   701   0.2  5000
 9 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.00000487   801   0.2  5000
10 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.00000522   901   0.2  5000
11 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y) -0.00000265  1001   0.2  5000
12 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y)  0.00000407  1101   0.2  5000
13 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y)  0.00000466  1201   0.2  5000
14 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y)  0.00000411  1301   0.2  5000
15 mix   x     y     f3(mix;x,y)  0.00000330  1401   0.2  5000


And we visualize the results (\(f_3\) as a function of tmix):

ggplot(f3_tmix, aes(tmix, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1500)) +
  labs(title = "f3(x, y; mix) as a function of admixture time (proportion = 20%, Ne = 5000)",
       subtitle = "[f3 < 0 is evidence of admixture]",
       x = "Time of admixture [generations ago]")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









From the trend presented by the trajectory of expected \(f_3\) values as a function of the admixture time, we can see that the statistic appears to lose power to detect admixture around 1000 generations “before present” (BP)—recall, that \(f_3\) admixture test is significant when it produces a negative value. Curiously, this is the case even though there’s quite a bit of admixture programmed (20%!).




What is the reason for the observation above? Under which conditions can we expect the \(f_3\) statistic to gain more power? Conversely, which of the parameters of our model would make a true scenario of admixture lead to a non-significant \(f_3\) value?
To answer these questions, fix the tmix parameter to 1000 generations ago and Ne at 5000 (i.e., the scenario in which we discovered that \(f_3\) loses power to detect admixture) , then run simulations across a range of admixture proportions prop between 0% and 50% gene flow. Does \(f_3\) pick up the admixture signal for any of these admixture proportions? What does it mean for the ability of \(f_3\) to detect gene flow in our models in general?






NoteClick to see the solution





Run the simulation for admixture proportions ranging between 0% and 50%, fixing the admixture time to the value of 1000 generations ago (i.e., a time point at which the \(f_3\) statistic stops giving us a negative value, i.e. it becomes statistically non-significant):

prop_grid <- seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.025)
f3_prop <- map_dfr(prop_grid, simulate_admixture, tmix = 1000, Ne = 5000)

When we visualize the results, we can see that — perhaps not unexpectedly — this loss of statistical power can be counterbalanced by increasing the admixture proportion:

ggplot(f3_prop, aes(prop, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(title = "f3(x, y; mix) as a function of admixture proportion (tsplit = 1000, Ne = 5000)",
       subtitle = "[f3 = 0 is interpreted as no evidence of admixture]",
       x = "Admixture proportion [0: no admixture, 0.5: 50% admixture]")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'













Similarly to how you investigated the detection power of \(f_3\) as a function of admixture proportion, repeat this analysis but now iterate with map_dfr() over a range of Ne values of the mixed population after admixture, leaving the prop parameter fixed at prop = 0.2 (again, the scenario in which \(f_3\) lost its admixture-detection power). What do you conclude based on this analysis? Does Ne have an impact on the \(f_3\) admixture detection? If it does, why?






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s run our final grid simulation batch, this time looping over \(N_e\) values in the admixed population and fixing the remaining two parameters tmix and prop at the values which originally got us non-significant \(f_3\) statistic (and, therefore, a false negative result on our admixture test):

Ne_grid <- seq(1000, 20000, by = 1000)
f3_Ne <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, simulate_admixture, tmix = 1000, prop = 0.2)

And visualize these results again:

ggplot(f3_Ne, aes(Ne, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1000, 20000)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "f3(x, y; mix) as a function of Ne (tsplit = 1000, Ne = 5000)",
       subtitle = "[f3 = 0 is interpreted as no evidence of admixture]",
       x = "Effective population size of the 'mix' population")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









In conclusion, we can confirm that the amount of drift (represented by the Ne parameter) really is what determines whether or not can \(f_3\) detect admixture for a given model (represented by a fixed tmix time and prop admixture proportion). In fact, once we reach a certain size of the admixed population, the \(f_3\) value reaches a stable level below zero.




After you’ve interpreted your results summarizing the expected behavior of the \(f_3\) statistic across a range of scenarios, take a look at the discussion surrounding equation 22 in this paper. Specifically, look at Figure 5B of the same paper! Does it look a bit familiar?
I hope these exercises (and the comparison to a real-world research result in theoretical population genetics linked above!) convinced you how powerful even very small simulation pipelines can be for benchmarking well-known summary statistics as well as for gaining confidence in the robustness of your inference results.
And these \(f_3\) simulations have been quite trivial compared to what is possible with simulation-based exploration and inference—stay tuned!

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Catching up
Here is a complete solution to the exercises so far, represented by a single reproducible R script admixture_simulation.R.






NoteClick to see the script admixture_simulation.R






library(slendr)
init_env()

library(dplyr)   # manipulating tabular data
library(ggplot2) # data visualization
library(purrr)   # convenient looping functions


############################################################
# generic function simulating population admixture with
# three parameters:
#   - tmix: admixture time
#   - prop: admixture proportion
#   - Ne: size of the admixed population

simulate_admixture <- function(tmix, prop, Ne) {
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 5000, time = 10000)
  x <- population("x", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)
  y <- population("y", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)

  # in this generalized model, admixture parameters for the mixed
  # population are parametrized as tmix, prop, and Ne
  mix <- population("mix", N = Ne, time = tmix + 1, parent = x)
  gf <- gene_flow(from = y, to = mix, start = tmix, end = tmix - 1, proportion = prop)
  
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, x, y, mix), gene_flow = gf, generation_time = 1)

  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(x, 20), list(y, 20), list(mix, 20))

  ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 25e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>% ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  ts_f3(ts, A = samples["mix"], B = samples["x"], C = samples["y"]) %>%
    mutate(tmix = tmix, prop = prop, Ne = Ne)
}


############################################################
# grid simulations over a range of admixture times

tmix_grid <- seq(1, 1500, by = 100)
f3_tmix <- map_dfr(tmix_grid, simulate_admixture, prop = 0.2, Ne = 5000)

ggplot(f3_tmix, aes(tmix, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1500)) +
  labs(title = "f3(x, y; mix) as a function of admixture time (proportion = 20%, Ne = 5000)",
       subtitle = "[f3 < 0 is evidence of admixture]",
       x = "Time of admixture [generations ago]")


############################################################
# grid simulations over a range of admixture proportions

prop_grid <- seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.025)
f3_prop <- map_dfr(prop_grid, simulate_admixture, tmix = 1000, Ne = 5000)

ggplot(f3_prop, aes(prop, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(title = "f3(x, y; mix) as a function of admixture proportion (tsplit = 1000, Ne = 5000)",
       subtitle = "[f3 < 0 is evidence of admixture]",

Ne_grid <- seq(1000, 20000, by = 1000)
f3_Ne <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, simulate_admixture, tmix = 1000, prop = 0.2)
