title: Between-population statistics
text:
Bonus exercise — Your own model
If you found yourself with extra time remaining for this chapter, I suggest the following:

Build a demographic model relevant for your research problem and population(s) of your interest. It could be a model you’ve inferred already in prior work, a model inspired by published literature that you’re familiar with, or a model from a completely different species that you’re interested in. If you’re not sure, try to implement a model of modern human history involving some populations from Africa, Eurasia, Americas, etc. (you kind find various inferred population trees on Google and use those as an inspiration).
Schedule the recording of a relevant set of individuals (perhaps a present-day reference panel, an ancient DNA time-series from historical populations, etc.).
Simulate a 50 Mb tree sequence with appropriate parameters for the average mutation and recombination rates, in order to get a representative genomic data set somewhat close to what you might have available in real-world sequences.
Practice computing of statistics introduced in the latest two chapters on the topic of tree-sequence statistics. This is purely a practice exercise, so feel free to improvise and experiment however you like.
Try to relate the simulated statistics to the equivalent (or close to equivalent) statistics you could find in the literature (by googling, looking up papers on demographic history of your population(s), searching Wikipedia, etc.). For instance, what’s the expected nucleotide diversity or heterozygosity estimated in real-world populations, their estimated \(N_e\) values, or some known pairwise \(F_{ST}\) or \(f_3\) statistics, etc.? Maybe you can try to compute them across the time-series (i.e., grouping individuals by their recording times, instead of their population assignments)? If your results don’t match the real-world values, let’s discuss among all of us why could this be.

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
text:
Theme of this chapter
In this chapter, we will delve a little bit into thinking about demographic histories (and about statistics we use to study those histories) through the lens of “tree thinking”—i.e., thinking in terms of genealogies recorded along the genome and, in particular, the branches in those genealogies. This fits the context of our work until this point quite naturally, particularly given the fact that the core component of slendr simulations is a tree sequence.
In the process, we will also change pace a bit, and use slendr as a sort of an “interactive popgen calculator” to quickly gain insights into population genetic statistics and explore them in an interactive way. Our main focus here will be on \(f\)-statistics and their interpretation through tracing paths along trees—particularly the \(f_4\) statistic—because they form such a crucial component of population genomics research.

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
text:
Literature

If you want to know much more about the technical background of \(f_3\) and \(f_4\) statistics and admixture proportion estimators like \(f_4\)-ratio, you can take a look at the following papers: Peter, 2016, Lipson 2020, and Patterson et al., 2012.
There are a number of software tools that can compute various \(f\) statistics on real data. If you’d like to compare simulated \(f\) statistics to empirical results, take a look at ADMIXTOOLS 2 or my own R package admixr.

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
section: Exercise: “Outgroup” \(f_3\) as a measure of overlap of tree paths
text:
Exercise: “Outgroup” \(f_3\) as a measure of overlap of tree paths
To ease into the problem of interpreting \(f\)-statistics as measures of overlapping paths in “population trees” or—when admixture comes into the picture—in “admixture graphs”, let’s briefly return to our familiar \(f_3\) statistic.
Restart your R session, then create a new script f_null.R and paste the following code into that script. As always, read through the code, try to build a mental model of what it’s going to do, then run it and compare your understanding with the generated visualization of the model.
(I know this is easy, but being able to read code quickly and efficiently is the best way to learn to spot bugs.)

library(slendr)
init_env()

# build a basic population tree structure
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

# compile the model and define recording of individuals
model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)
schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 5))

# plot the model to check its correctness visually
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)

# simulate 10 Mb of genomic data for later exploration
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)


Now, consider the model implemented in our script f_null.R, visualized below:









We know from the paper describing the theory of \(f\)-statistics and from our brief introduction that:

\(f_2(A, B)\) statistic measures the branch length between A and B (two individuals, two groups of individuals, two populations, etc.), and similarly
\(f_3(C; A, B)\) statistic is defined as the branch length which connects the internal most recent common ancestor node of A and B with the lineage C,
\(f_4\) (which we will discuss later) has a similar interpretation.

(These three ideas can be seen graphically in Figure 1 of that linked paper.)
Another thing established in the paper is the fact that any \(f\)-statistic can be expressed as a linear combination of multiple \(f_2\) statistics. In other words, you can “build” them by adding or subtracting multiple individual \(f_2\) branch lengths. If you’re not familiar with linear algebra, this might sound a bit obscure, but the idea is simple. More concretely, for instance, equation (20b) in the same paper states the following, which decomposes an \(f_3\) statistic into a composite of simpler \(f_2\) statistics (this is what “linear combination” basically is):
\[f_3(A; B, C) = \frac{1}{2} (f_2(A, C) + f_2(A, B) - f_2(B, C))\]

Draw a sketch of the population model (of populations p1, p2, p3, etc.) on a piece of paper, then trace by hand the paths indicated by the three \(f_2\) statistics in this equation on that sketch. When you “add” and “subtract” paths based on the equation (graphically by hand!), do you arrive at the definition of “outgroup” \(f_3\) as branch length from A and B towards the outgroup, as we described it in point 2. above?

When I was writing this chapter, I made a mistake in the equation above, which I discovered only after I wrote a quick simulation to double-check that the equation is correct. Let’s retrace my steps here because it shows why even very quick simulations can be really useful (almost like a “popgen calculator”!).
Let’s move to R. Use the function ts_f2() to implement this equation in code, computing a “homemade” \(f_3(A = p4; B = p1, C = p2)\) statistic which you just solved on paper, and compare it to the result you get if you run the computation using the ts_f3() function by slendr. Do you get the same result using both methods, and therefore verifying that the equation is correct?
Hint: You can either refer to entire populations in the ts_f2() like you did until now, or you can also use as A, B, and C single individuals (i.e., “pop4_1”, “pop1_1”, etc.).






NoteClick to see the solution





First let’s get our groups of individuals in the tree sequence so that we can refer to populations more easily:

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
s

$p1
[1] "p1_1" "p1_2" "p1_3" "p1_4" "p1_5"

$p2
[1] "p2_1" "p2_2" "p2_3" "p2_4" "p2_5"

$p3
[1] "p3_1" "p3_2" "p3_3" "p3_4" "p3_5"

$p4
[1] "p4_1" "p4_2" "p4_3" "p4_4" "p4_5"

$px
[1] "px_1" "px_2" "px_3" "px_4" "px_5"


Let’s compose a “homemade” \(f_3\) statistic as a linear combination of \(f_2\) statistics as given by the equation:

homemade_f3 <- 1/2 * (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"])$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"])$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"])$f2
)
homemade_f3

[1] 0.0001119332


Finally, let’s compute \(f_3\) using the “official” built-in slendr function:

simulated_f3 <- ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"])
simulated_f3

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  A     B     C     statistic          f3
  <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>           <dbl>
1 p4    p1    p2    f3(p4;p1,p2) 0.000112


You can see that the ts_f3() implementation gives basically the same value as our “homemade” implementation based on a linear combination of \(f_2\) statistics, just as predicted by the underlying mathematical equation!

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
text:
Exercise: Mutations versus branches
Do you recall how I told you that you don’t have to add mutations to your tree sequence ts, and still be able to compute population genetic statistics? But that you can safely add them with ts_mutate() anyway?
The reason this works is because some very smart people figured out a mathematical duality between mutation-based and branch-based statistics—it actually doesn’t matter which way we compute our statistics, they give mathematically the same result in terms of theoretical statistical expectations (i.e., expectations of what happen in real data).

Repeat the previous exercise, but this time specify mode = "branch" in all your ts_f3() and ts_f2() commands. I suggest that you make a copy of your ts_f3() and ts_f2()-based code in your f_null.R script and and modify the copies for easier comparison of the results. What numbers do you get compared to the results of the previous exercise in terms of their scale? Can you relate those values to what your population tree model visualization indicates (in terms of branch lenghts)? Look at your sketch with pen and paper again if this helps in putting your results in clearer context (particularly with regards to split times).






NoteClick to see the solution





Here are the two code chunks from the previous solution computed by setting mode = "branch":

ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"], mode = "branch")

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  A     B     C     statistic        f3
  <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>         <dbl>
1 p4    p1    p2    f3(p4;p1,p2) 10839.



homemade_f3 <- (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], mode = "branch")$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"], mode = "branch")$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"], mode = "branch")$f2
) / 2

homemade_f3

[1] 10839.42


We can see that when we specify mode = "branch", the returned values of \(f\) statistics correspond to the real branch lengths in terms of times in generations! To see this, just take a look at your model sketch again, counting how much time there’s between split times. This is quite cool because as we discussed, the mathematical expectation of \(f_3\) statistic does, in fact, represent the overlap of paths in a tree going from p1 and p2 to the outgroup p4:












Hopefully, you can now appreciate that there’s nothing magical about \(f\) statistics. Even though their practical interpretation can get sometimes complicated, internally they always boil down to tracing paths through population trees in order to obtain statistical expectations of allele frequency correlations between lineages under study (interpreted as branch lengths), easily visualized by tracing paths through population trees.
In a way, setting mode = "branch" can be understood as instructing slendr to compute the results — in this case, of the \(f_3\) statistic — in “real time units” (in the case of this simple model, in generations).

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
section: Exercise: Basic intuition into the \(f_4\) statistic
text:
Exercise: Basic intuition into the \(f_4\) statistic
Now let’s finally dig into exploring the most critical component of population genetics research (particularly in the context of ancient DNA)—the venerable \(f_4\)-statistic, formally established by Nick Patterson and David Reich in 2012.
From the intuitive follow-up paper on \(f\)-statistics by Benjamin Peter, we know that (in a very similar way to \(f_2\) and \(f_3\)) the \(f_4(W, X; Y, Z)\) statistic can be interpreted as the overlap between the paths in a tree connecting the pairs W-X and Y-Z, as is demonstrated in Figure 1 of the linked paper.
That said, what value does any given \(f_4\) statistic actually gives you depends on the (in practice, hidden) underlying demographic model which determines how populations are related—this is what we need to infer—and also what individuals assign into each of the four positions of the \(f_4\) “quartet configuration”.

Knowing the relationships between populations encoded by the tree model programmed in your script f_null.R and the interpretation of the \(f_4\) statistic, what is the expected value of \(f_4(p1, px; p3, p4)\) for this model? Try to answer by taking a look at the sketch of your model and tracing the path overlaps between p1-px and p3-p4 pairs, then compute the statistic on a ts simulated data with the ts_f4() function to verify your intuition. Does your simulation give you the exact result you might expect based on the visualization of the model alone? If it doesn’t give you the exact expected result, why could this be?






Noteclick to see the solution





As we can see below, \(f\)-statistics theory tells us that the value should be zero, but without having a reference baseline, we get a number which is very tiny (the value in the f4 column). But how tiny would it have to be to be “basically zero”?

ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  W     X     Y     Z     statistic                f4
  <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>                 <dbl>
1 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4) 0.000000364


The reason we didn’t get exactly zero is stochastic noise of any evolutionary process, which means that that along a genome (even a small one, only 10 Mb of simulated sequence) there are many possible trees. Sometimes, incomplete lineage sorting will lead to genealogical trees which do not fit the expected “well-behaved” population tree like the one we see when we run plot_model(). We will see examples of this at the end of this chapter.
That said, gene trees that don’t fit the overall population trees will tend to “average out”, particularly when we look across many different regions of the genome—this is why the simulated \(f_4\) gets very close to zero in practice.




As suggested in the solution above, the reason we don’t get a perfectly zero expected value of the \(f_4\) is because of ILS and stochasticity. Let’s test this hypothesis now.
First, evaluate ts in your R console and note how many trees do you have in your 10 Mb tree-sequence.
Now, restart your R session (Session -> Restart R). Then, temporarily change the N of all populations in your model to 1 and re-run your script to get a new ts and compute the same \(f_4\) statistic again. \(N_e = 1\) implies a ludicrously high amount of drift, which should eliminate ILS completely, giving us \(f_4\) close to its mathematical expectation of zero. Is this true in your new simulation? And how many trees does your tree sequence have with this high amount of drift?






NoteClick to see the solution





We changed all N sizes to 1, then we rerun the entire script f_statistics.R again:

library(slendr)
init_env()

# !!!
# note the temporary change to N = 1
# !!!
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 5))

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

Now let’s compute the \(f_4\) again on the ts tree sequence produced by this extreme model. When we do this, we see that the value really is zero, exactly as the theory predicts:

ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  W     X     Y     Z     statistic          f4
  <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>           <dbl>
1 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4)     0


Indeed, when we type ts into the R console, we see that it only contains 4 individual trees compared to the previous count of 4199, consistent with an absolutely extreme amounts of genetic drift in your model:

ts

╟───────────────┼───────────╢
║Sequence Length│ 10,000,000║

Of course, changing \(N_e\) to value of 1 as we did above is a drastic measure of only theoretical utility. We could hardly get away with doing that, if we wanted to use simulations to make a point in our research paper.
How do we deal with the unavoidable stochasticity in our simulations then? This wasn’t much of a problem in exercises in the previous chapters, but we need the way to solve this to be able to get useful, applicable results.
Let’s look into this now.

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
section: Exercise: Reducing stochastic noise via simulation replicates
text:
Exercise: Reducing stochastic noise via simulation replicates
First, set the N sizes of your populations in your model from 1 back to 1000, then re-run your script to make sure the original model is compiled (ideally by restarting R again).
As a means to tame the stochasticity and help meaningful statistical patterns stand out, I recently implemented a new slendr function ts_replicates(), specifically for this workshop! The way it works is like this:

ts_replicate(
  n = <number of replicates to simulate>,
  {
    # ...
    # a block of slendr code wrapped in { ... } containing a ts simulation
    # and a statistical computation we want to run in given replicates
    # ...
  }
)


Take a look at its manual page under ?ts_replicates, then use it to run 10 replicate simulations of the \(f_4\) statistic above (the one which should give us exactly zero value, but didn’t), saving the result to variable df. What format does the result have? When you visualize the distribution of \(f_4\) values across all 10 replicates, are they more interpretable in terms of the statistical expectation for this particular \(f_4\) “quartet”?


Note: If you want to speed up the replicate simulation, note that ?ts_replicate allows running multiple simulations in parallel.






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s how we can modify the “template” above to answer this question:

df <- ts_replicate(

  # run 10 replicates ...
  n = 10,

  # ... of the following block of code...
  {

  # ... which first simulates a tree sequence ...
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # ... and then computes a data frame with the given f4 statistic ...
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])

  } # ... the function automatically binds all data frames into single one
)

We can see that we get the same format of the data frame as normally produced by the ts_f4() function, except with a new column rep added, indicating a replicate number.

df

   <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>                   <dbl> <int>

 4 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4)  0.00000112       4
 5 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4) -0.00000108       5
 6 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4) -0.000000728      6
 7 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4)  0.000000392      7
 8 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4) -0.00000095       8

10 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4)  0.0000000750    10


This means we can visualize their distribution easily like this, for example:

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")








As we can see, when we run multiple replicates of the simulation, we are able to “control” the stochastic noise a bit, making the expected pattern stand out more clearly: we see that the expected value of f4(p1,px;p3,p4) is really zero (up to that unavoidable stochastic noise shown by the scatter of individual replicate values around zero).

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
text:
Exercise: Other \(f_4\) “quartets”
Of course, \(f_4(p1, px; p3, p4)\) is only one possible “quartet configuration”.
Expand your 10 replicates simulation \(f_4(p1, px; p3, p4)\) by adding the computation of \(f_4(p1, p3; px, p4)\) and \(f_4(p1, p4; px, p3)\) in the same { ... } block provided to ts_replicate() (making sure you rbind() all three data resulting frames together at the end of the { ... } block).
How would you compare the interpretation of the three \(f_4\) statistics against one another? Again, use sketching of paths on a population tree on paper to try to figure it out first based on the definition of what \(f_4\) between the given two pairs of lineages indicate, then compare your understanding to what you see when you visualize the distributions of those three statistics.
Hint: This requires some ggplot2 visualization knowledge. Feel free to take a peek at my solution to learn how to plot the results, or just my own visualization for interpreting the differences between the three statistics.






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s add the computation of all three \(f_4\) statistics in the same replicate simulation pipeline:

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  # instead of computing one f4 like before, we compute all three and then
  # bind the three data frames into a single one
  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"]), # 1st f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p4"]), # 2nd f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"])  # 3rd f4
  )
})

Again, we get a data frame with multiple replicates for each of the three statistics:

df

# A tibble: 30 × 7
   W     X     Y     Z     statistic                 f4   rep
   <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>                  <dbl> <int>
 1 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4)  0.000000843     1
 2 p1    p3    px    p4    f4(p1,p3;px,p4)  0.0000131       1
 3 p1    p4    px    p3    f4(p1,p4;px,p3)  0.0000123       1
 4 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4) -0.000000489     2
 5 p1    p3    px    p4    f4(p1,p3;px,p4)  0.00000763      2
 6 p1    p4    px    p3    f4(p1,p4;px,p3)  0.00000812      2
 7 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4)  0.000000329     3
 8 p1    p3    px    p4    f4(p1,p3;px,p4)  0.0000107       3
 9 p1    p4    px    p3    f4(p1,p4;px,p3)  0.0000103       3
10 p1    px    p3    p4    f4(p1,px;p3,p4)  0.00000128      4
# ℹ 20 more rows


From the mathematical definition of \(f_4\) as internal branch lengths between two pairs of lineages in a given “quartet” and knowing the topological structure of our population tree, we can predict that the first \(f_4\) is expected to be zero (which is what we established earlier), and the other two \(f_4\) statistics are expected to have the same value representing the internal branch length connecting two pairs in the “quartet”.
This is exactly what we see in our results:

ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")












Make a copy of your ts_replicate() code computing the three \(f_4\) statistics and modify it by setting mode = "branch", as we did before, perhaps changing df to df_branch in this copied code for easier comparison. Recall that mode = "branch" instructs slendr’s internal statistical machinery to use “model time units” (here, generations) in computing the results based on branches, instead of mutations. When you visualize the three \(f_4\) statistics computed in this way, do you see this being reflected in the scale (and meaning) of the numbers which you get back?






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s save the result in a new data frame df_branch:

df_branch <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"), # 1st f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"), # 2nd f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")  # 3rd f4
  )
})

When we visualize the results, we do indeed see that the f4 column contains the expected branch lengths expressed in real generation times! Here are the results plotted alongside the model using the package cowplot so that the branch length times can be read more easily:

library(cowplot) # get access to the plot_grid() function

plot_grid(
  # first panel:
  plot_model(model),

  # second panel:
  ggplot(df_branch, aes(statistic, f4)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    geom_jitter() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed"),

  # plot both panels in two rows:
  nrow = 2
)

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
text:
Catching up
This was a lot of work! If you want to check in with the state of our \(f\)-statistics exploratory simulation script f_null.R, here it is in the form which showcases the most important results from this chapter so far:






NoteClick to see the entire script






##################################################
# load the necessary packages

library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 5))

##################################################
# simulate replicates of the three f4 statistics
# (based on branches)

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")
  )
})

##################################################
# visualize branch-based f4 statistics alongside
# the corresponding demographic model (note that
# ggplot figures can be stored in variables!)

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_df <- ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_df, nrow = 2)

p_panels

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
section: Exercise: Interpreting \(f_4\) as an admixture hypothesis test
text:
Exercise: Interpreting \(f_4\) as an admixture hypothesis test
Admittedly, thinking about \(f\) statistics as measures of allele frequency correlations between populations and interpreting them as overlapping branch lengths is intellectually interesting in terms of population genetics theory, but in practice, they are most famous (and most famously used) as admixture tests.
Create a new script f_admixture.R and copy my solutions to the exercises in this chapter available under the “Catching up” section above into that script. This is just to get the same starting point. Restart your R session (Session -> Restart R) then skim through this script and re-run it. Having gone through the exercises, the code should look somewhat familiar and the visualization you obtain by typing out p_panels into your R console (the branch lengths encoded by the three \(f_4\) statistics we studied) should make sense.






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the final visualization of the three \(f_3\) statistics for easier reference as you work on the following exercise.













Right now our script f_admixture.R doesn’t have any admixture. It still contains what we established in this chapter so far: a statistical null model of “nothing interesting happened in the demographic history in terms of potential admixture”, as is reflected in the \(f_4\) values we obtained–most importantly in the “null hypothesis” statistic \(f_4(p1,px;p3,p4)\) being zero.
Introduce the following two changes to the f_admixture.R script to turn it into an admixture model:

Program a gene_flow() event gf, introducing 20% gene-flow from p3 to px between 400 and 300 generations ago.
Add this gf event into the model compilation step executed by compile_model().

With the steps 1. and 2. done, your model now includes admixture. Re-run the script again, and inspect the final visualization obtained by typing out p_panels into your R console. You should see an admixture edge added to your population tree.

How does admixture from p3 to px affect the branch lengths compared to the previous model f_null.R when you visualize the replicates for each of the three \(f_4\) statistics from the admixture model? Pay particular attention to the \(f_4(p1,px;p3,p4)\) statistic which had an expected value of zero before—does it still have a zero value? If not, why, and what does it tell us about it utility to study admixture histories?






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s only the final visualization of the figure in the p_panel variable:









As we can see, because of the admixture event, our previously tree-like population model is no longer tree. In the tree model without an admixture edge, there was no path overlap between the pairs p1-px and p3-p4, which is why the \(f_4(p1,px;p3,p4)\) statistic was zero.
Admixture is a violation of “treeness”, because “mathematical” trees are not allowed to have edges (they effectively create “loops” in the trees)—structures which do have edges are instead called “admixture graphs”. This is why the statistic now significantly deviates from zero (and is negative).
This is exactly why \(f_4\) is useful as a statistical hypothesis test of admixture—if a population quartet is from a truly tree-like model, this statistic will always necessarily be zero; conversely, it can only ever be non-zero if the underlying model (usually hidden, in real-world applications) involves admixture which violates “treeness”.

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
text:
Exercise: Estimating admixture proportions
From the little simulation and tree-doodling experiments, we now have a sense of how \(f\) statistics mathematically quantify allele frequency correlations between lineages of population trees and how they can be interpreted as the amounts of overlaps of paths traced along branches of those trees.
We also have an idea how different patterns emerge in \(f_4\) statistic expectations when gene-flow is introduced into population trees, adding admixture edges to them and turning them into so-called “admixture graphs”.
It turns out that the same principles allow us to not just test the hypothesis of whether an admixture event happened in the history of our samples, but also estimate the proportion of ancestry derived from this admixture—a concept known as \(f_4\)-ratio statistics.

The theory of \(f_4\)-ratios can get quite complex, but let’s try to get an idea about its internal workings using a very simple example and build up from there. We’ll end up inventing the \(f_4\)-ratio statistic from scratch!
Let’s consider our model again and set a goal to estimate how much ancestry of px came from p3 (or how much came from p2 into px—these are complementary, of course). Imagine tracing a path through the population from px to p2 through the tree. Draw a fresh sketch of our five-population model on paper, and trace this px-p2 path on it.
How many such paths can we take through the tree?















NoteClick to see the solution





There are two paths:

We could either go from px “to the right” and walk through the tree through the p3 population and them “loop over” into the p2 population.
Alternatively, we could go “to the left” and arrive to p2 “directly” through the population split of px from p2.

We only have those two possibilities, because we know that the genetic ancestry of px is effectively derived from admixture between p2 and p3 lineages.
(In fact, because this is a simulation, we even know that 20% of the genome of px comes from p3 and 80% comes from p2, meaning that 20% of our paths will go through the p3 lineage.)




How many px to p2 paths would we have available if there wasn’t any admixture in the model?






NoteClick to see the solution





If our model didn’t have an admixture edge it would be a simple tree, meaning that we could only trace one path from px to p2 “directly” through the population split of px from p2.




Now that we’ve established that there are two possible paths from px to p2 in our admixture model, what is the interpretation of \(f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)\) at any given locus of the genome? What would be the possible values of this \(f_4\) in this situation? Again, try to use pen and paper to figure it out based on the knowledge of \(f_4\) as a measures of internal branches in a tree.
Hint: Remember that we’ve established that there are two possible paths from px to p2 in the tree, depending on whether px has a genetic ancestry coming from p2 or p3 at a given locus of the genome.






NoteClick to see the solution





The \(f_4\) statistic in question could give two possible results, depending on the paths 1. or 2. taken (as explain in the previous section):

In the first potential path, \(f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)\) would be the length of the shared internal branch in the tree between pairs p1-p4 and p2-px (or, effectively, p2-p3, because that locus in px originated in p3 due to admixture).
In the second potential path, \(f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)\) would be zero! This is because in such a situation, there’s no overlap between pairs p1-p4 and p2-p3 in the tree—and so there’s no such internal branch.





Now for the final punchline!
You’ve already established that one of the two interpretations of \(f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)\) describes the internal branch in the tree separating the pairs p1-p4 and px-p2, which exists for the parts of the genome which px inherited from p3 (the other interpretation giving a value of zero, by definition).
What is the interpretation of \(f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)\)? Again, sketch the internal path represented by this \(f_4\) statistic in your tree model on paper.

Finally, what happens if you would take the value produced by \(f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)\) and divided it by \(f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)\), i.e. what is the interpretation of the following equation?
\[\frac{f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)}{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)}\]






NoteClick to see the solution





As we’ve shown in the first part of this exercise, if we want to model the ancestry of px as an admixture of \(\alpha\) proportion from p3 and \((1 -
\alpha)\) proportion from p2, we can effectively decompose \(f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)\) into two possible outcomes corresponding two two possible quantities:

one of them is zero (and happens in \((1 - \alpha)\) proportion of cases),
the other one gives the internal branch length (and happens in \(\alpha\) proportion of cases).

We can then use this fact to expand the ratio given in the equation above like this (using the fact that the red-highlighted branch length is zero, leaving the rest of the fraction to cancel each other):
\[
\frac{f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)}{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)} =
\frac{(1 - \alpha) f_4(p1,p4;p2,p2) + \alpha f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)}{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)} =
\frac{\textcolor{red}{\cancelto{0}{(1-\alpha)f_4(p1,p4;p2,p2)}} + \alpha \cancel{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)}}{\cancel{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)}} =
\alpha
\]
And hurray, just like this, we invented the famous \(f_4\)-ratio estimator for ancestry proportion!




There’s one thing to be smart and logical, there’s one thing to be able to derive an equation (or be handed one equation from a paper or a textbook). Trusting and understanding the equation is another matter—that’s when simulations can be very useful again.
Use the equation for the \(f_4\)-ratio estimator of ancestry proportion to write a new code chunk in your f_admixture.R script which will simulate the values of this estimator expected from our admixture model using a ratio two individual ts_f4() statistics, specifying the quartet configuration accordingly. Then visualize the admixture proportion thus computed—did your estimator recover the known value of 20% of admixture?
If you want an extra challenge, it turns out there are multiple variations of how the ancestry proportion can be estimated. Try to find them, add them to your ts_replicate() code and compare them to one another by visualizing their distributions across all replicates.






NoteClick to see the solution





I managed to come up with three possible \(f_4\)-ratio variations, all three programmed and benchmarked below:

Variant number 1 is the one we derived together, based on tracing the path from px to p2 through population p3 (this is predicted to estimate 20% ancestry).
Variant number 2 is the complement to the first variant which traces the ancestry from px to p3 through population p2 (and therefore is expected to estimate 80% ancestry).
Variant number 3 is a little strange and I came up with it by accident when I was developing the very first \(f_4\) ratio exercise. Notice that although it does produce the correct 20% expectation, it shows a much higher variance (i.e., much more statistical noise).


props <- ts_replicate(
  n = 50,
  {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
    
  # variant #1 -- this is the variant we derived together
  num1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p2"])$f4
  den1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p2"])$f4
  prop1 <- num1 / den1
  
  # variant #2
  num2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  den2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  prop2 <- num2 / den2

  # variant #3 (a weird one?)
  num3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"])$f4
  den3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"])$f4
  prop3 <- - num3 / den3
    
  # create a data frame with different variants
  data.frame(
    proportion = c("variant1", "variant2", "variant3 (weird one?)"),
    value = c(prop1, prop2, prop3)
  )
  },
  parallel = parallel::detectCores() - 1
)

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_f4ratios <- ggplot(props, aes(value, color = proportion)) +
    geom_density() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.2, 0.8), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(title = "Simulation-based validation of f4-ratio ancestry estimates",
         subtitle = "(three different variations of f4-ratios are shown)",
         x = "ancestry proportion") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_ratios <- plot_grid(p_model, p_f4ratios, nrow = 2)

p_ratios








Note that there’s still a lot of variance and noise. In a practical setting, we would run many more simulation replicates (100 or even more) for genomes much longer than just 10 Mb (for instance, even 100 Mb). We don’t do this here because those simulations would take too long to do on a normal laptop.

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
text:
Catching up
This was even more work! And no wonder—a simulation-based analysis like this one could easily be part of a real research paper. In fact, many studies which introduced these theoretical concepts used these simulations as proof-of-principle, and increasing number of applications include them for benchmarking and validation of results. Now you know how to do these things as well!
If you want to see the state of the final f_admixture.R script, you can find it below.






NoteClick to see the entire script






##################################################
# load the necessary packages

library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p3, to = px, start = 400, end = 300, proportion = 0.2)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px),
  gene_flow = gf,
  generation_time = 1
)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

##################################################
# implement variations of f4-ratio estimates and
# benchmark them with simple simulations

props <- ts_replicate(
  n = 50,
  {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
    
  # variant #1 -- this is the variant we derived together
  num1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p2"])$f4
  den1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p2"])$f4
  prop1 <- num1 / den1
  
  # variant #2
  num2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  den2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  prop2 <- num2 / den2

  # variant #3 (a weird one?)
  num3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"])$f4
  den3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"])$f4
  prop3 <- - num3 / den3
    
  # create a data frame with different variants
  data.frame(
    proportion = c("variant1", "variant2", "variant3 (weird one?)"),
    value = c(prop1, prop2, prop3)
  )
  },
  parallel = parallel::detectCores() - 1
)

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_f4ratios <- ggplot(props, aes(value, color = proportion)) +
    geom_density() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.2, 0.8), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(title = "Simulation-based validation of f4-ratio ancestry estimates",
         subtitle = "(three different variations of f4-ratios are shown)",
         x = "ancestry proportion") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_f4ratios, nrow = 2)

p_panels

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
text:
Exercise: What are tree sequences?
We’ve mentioned the concept of a “tree sequence” many times but until this chapter, we haven’t considered tree-thinking very explicitly. Indeed, for most of our daily practical work, we don’t need to be aware of the underlying tree-sequence data that much, but it’s always a good idea to know what’s going on behind the scenes of the methods that we use. Let’s take a small peek at what actually is hiding behind our familiar ts objects in practice. This section will be more like a demonstration rather than a “serious exercise”, just in case you’re curious about this topic.

When you type ts into your R console, you’ll get a summary of the most important characteristics in your data. For instance, consider a small 1 Mb tree-sequence simulation like this, and note the number of trees, the number of edges, nodes, and mutations:

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 1))

ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule, random_seed = 42) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = 42)

ts

╚═══════════╧════╧═════════╧════════════╝



We can extract a single tree at a given index using the function ts_tree(). (Note that because slendr ties into the Python module tskit behind the scenes, indexing into the tree sequence starts at 0.) This doesn’t give us much information though—it’s just an opaque object in computer memory, but we don’t see anything interesting when we type the tree variable into the R console:

tree <- ts_tree(ts, i = 0)
tree

<tskit.trees.Tree object at 0x11b037b30>



We can use the built-in slendr helper function ts_draw() to visualize these tree objects. For instance, here’s how we can visualize the 0th (i.e., the first) tree in our small tree sequence. Note that by setting labels = TRUE, we can see individuals’ names at the leaves of the tree, as well as the fact that each individual is represented by two leaves (one for each of its two chromosomes).

ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))









Take a few minutes visualizing different trees, perhaps starting from 0th and going forward, until you get bored!

As you do this, notice that “neighboring” trees tend to be quite similar (why do you think this is?).
Can you find an example of a tree which fits our underlying population tree model?
How about trees which clearly “contradict” this model? Can you find any?
How about a tree which would show evidence of gene flow from p3 to px we programmed in our model? Can you find one?
You might encounter red cross signs plotted on the trees—what do they represent?

The outcome of an evolutionary simulation is completely random, so don’t get too frustrated if you don’t find lots of meaningful information while doing this. At the very least, when you explore the trees along the tree sequence, even for a small section of a genome like 1 Mb in this case, it makes you appreciate just how complex real-world evolutionary processes are.
If you want to explore the exact same tree-sequence that I had, you can download it with the following commands and use it instead of your simulated ts object:






NoteClick to read my own tree sequence ts instead






ts_path <- tempfile()
options(timeout = 600)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodkan/simgen/refs/heads/main/files/introgression/example.trees", destfile = ts_path, mode = "wb")
ts <- ts_read(file = ts_path, model = model)










NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s what I found after a couple of minutes of visualizing different trees in my tree sequence:

A neat and tidy genealogy which is completely concordant with our population tree (take a look at the tip labels with population names and compare this tree to the overall population tree model we worked with in this chapter):


i <- 203
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i)
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))








We can also see that the tree immediately after this one is basically the same. This is because of a single (ancient) recombination event which only affected one branch in the tree, but the remainder of the genealogy stays the same (because recombination didn’t affect those individuals’ ancestors):

i <- 204
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i)
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))









A tree showing a clear evidence of introgression from p3 into px:


i <- 243
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i)
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))









Another locus in the genome carries a tree which is an utter mess and doesn’t seem to be similar to our underlying population tree model at all:


i <- 114
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i)
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))








Oh, and the red crosses represent mutations!



I hope that this little exercise illustrates nicely just how much work population genetic statistics do for us in understanding the hidden truth behind real-world evolutionary processes—they do this by aggregating massive amounts of convoluted genealogical data resulting from these processes, and help us extract and see meaningful patterns in them.

title: Tree thinking and \(f\) statistics
section: Bonus exercise (if you want a programming challenge)
text:
Bonus exercise (if you want a programming challenge)
When playing with \(f\)-statistics in this chapter, you’ve probably noticed various symmetries in \(f_4\) (but also other \(f\)-statistics) depending on the arrangement of their “configuration” (order of populations). As a trivial example, an \(f_3(A; B, C)\) and \(f_3(A; C, B)\) will give you exactly the same value.
Try to figure out how many unique \(f_4\) values involving a single quartet (for instance, quartets involving different permutations of p1, p2, p3, and p4 populations) are there. How about how many absolute values? You could answer this by drawing and doodling on paper, but try to use computer simulations to do this too! You can program whatever demographic model you’d like for this purpose—the specifics don’t matter much as long as the model has some four populations involved.






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s a complete script with comments explaining the most important steps:

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

library(slendr)
init_env()

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

# install a combinatorics R package:
# install.packages("combinat")
library(combinat)

# these are the four samples we can create quartet combinations from:
quartet <- c("p1_1", "p2_1", "p3_1", "p4_1")

# this is how we can generate all permutations:
quartets <- permn(quartet)
quartets

title: Haplotype-based methods
text:
Theme of this chapter
All of our exercises so far focused on population genetic statistics which are generally thought about in terms of allele frequencies and allele frequency correlations. However, one class of modeling tools implemented in slendr which are also extremely useful are methods based on haplotypes—i.e., continuous segments of DNA inherited from generation to generation while being broken up by the process of recombination.
To make this session a little more relaxed compared to previous exercises, this chapter presents these techniques as a set of “recipes” rather than extensive exercises. The primary goal is to conclude our exercise sessions with a few more tools before we switch gears and start implementing modeling workflows for your own projects or work through some of the few suggested case studies.

title: Haplotype-based methods
text:
Preparation
Take a look at the following basic admixture model, and save it as haplotypes.R. Note also the presence of a small helper function I provided (you don’t have to study it, although it should look familiar if you’ve done the tidyverse and ggplot2 parts of this workbook):






NoteClick to see the entire script






##################################################
# simple admixture demographic model
library(slendr)
init_env()

popZ <- population("popZ", time = 3000, N = 500)
popX <- population("popX", time = 1500, N = 2000, parent = popZ)
popY <- population("popY", time = 1500, N = 10000, parent = popZ)

gf <- gene_flow(from = popX, to = popY, proportion = 0.2, start = 500, end = 499)

model <- compile_model(list(popZ, popX, popY), generation_time = 1, gene_flow = gf)

schedule <- rbind(
  schedule_recording(model, times = seq(1400, 0, by = -200), list(popY, 10)),
  schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(popX, 10), list(popZ, 10))
)
  
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 100e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule, random_seed = 42) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = 42)

samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

##################################################
# a helper function to plot admixture tracts

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(scales)

plot_tracts <- function(tracts, ind) {
  ind_tracts <- filter(tracts, name %in% ind) %>%
    mutate(chr = paste0(name, "\nchr. ", haplotype)) %>%
    mutate(chr = factor(chr, levels = unique(chr[order(node_id)])))

  ggplot(ind_tracts) +
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = left, xmax = right, ymin = 1, ymax = 2, fill = name),
              linewidth = 1) +
    labs(x = "coordinate along a chromosome [bp]") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          panel.border = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) +
    facet_grid(chr ~ .) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = comma)
}




Here is what this model look like. Note particularly the “ancient DNA time series” we simulated in popY and the admixture from popX into popY:

plot_model(model, schedule = schedule, proportions = TRUE)

title: Haplotype-based methods
section: Exercise: Local ancestry inference (LAI) with ts_tracts()
text:
Exercise: Local ancestry inference (LAI) with ts_tracts()
As mentioned above, we’ve learned a lot about admixture tests based on allele frequency correlations, namely \(f\)-statistics. Although very powerful, there are situations where they either lose inference power or they don’t allow us to answer deeper questions we might be also interested in.
For instance, what if we want to detect not only if or how much admixture happened, but where in the genome can we detect continuous admixture blocks?
A wide range of software methods called Local Ancestry Inference (LAI) have been developed do do exactly this, each with their strengths and weaknesses. For an overview, see this preprint which I put together with a former PhD student about LAI methods (fun fact: slendr is what made this work possible!).
On the simulation side, slendr provides a function ts_tracts(), which can extract the exact coordinates of admixture tracts resulting an admixture event. This is extremely useful both for simulation-based inference, but also for benchmarking software methods, picking which method gives the most accurate answer in our scenario of interest, etc.

If you have a simulated tree sequence ts (such as the one simulated by your script haplotypes.R), you can obtain admixture tracts by providing a so-called “census time” to the function ts_tracts() (this is a slightly strange name for a low-level technical concept corresponding to the time of gene-flow we want to focus on). In case of our model, set this census to 500 generations and add the following command to your script haplotypes.R, then run it. What’s the format of the data it gives you? Can you guess what sort of information it contains by looking through it?






NoteClick to see the solution






tracts <- ts_tracts(ts, census = 500)

When you look at the output of this function, you seen that it’s a plain data frame with many columns which will be familiar to you:

head(tracts)

# A tibble: 6 × 10
  name    haplotype  time pop   source_pop     left   right length source_pop_id
  <chr>       <int> <dbl> <chr> <fct>         <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>         <dbl>
1 popY_51         1   400 popY  popX        3203460  6.14e6 2.94e6             1
2 popY_51         1   400 popY  popX        6463080  8.31e6 1.84e6             1
3 popY_51         1   400 popY  popX       11598709  1.28e7 1.15e6             1
4 popY_51         1   400 popY  popX       23655661  2.38e7 1.16e5             1
5 popY_51         1   400 popY  popX       26049625  2.72e7 1.15e6             1
6 popY_51         1   400 popY  popX       40089367  4.57e7 5.56e6             1
# ℹ 1 more variable: node_id <dbl>


For instance, name indicates the name of the individual carrying a given admixture tract derived from admixture from source population source_pop with genomic coordinates between left and right.




Can you guess the meaning of the haplotype column? How many of them are there for any given individual? You can use your tidyverse magic to answer this.






NoteClick to see the solution





This finds the haplotype number and node ID for each individual:

tracts %>% group_by(name) %>% distinct(haplotype, node_id)

# A tibble: 60 × 3
# Groups:   name [30]
   name    haplotype node_id
   <chr>       <int>   <dbl>
 1 popY_51         1     100
 2 popY_51         2     101
 3 popY_52         1     102
 4 popY_52         2     103
 5 popY_53         1     104
 6 popY_53         2     105
 7 popY_54         1     106
 8 popY_54         2     107
 9 popY_55         1     108
10 popY_55         2     109
# ℹ 50 more rows


Haplotype is basically equivalent to “chromosome” in this case. Because each simulated slendr individual is diploid, we get one “chromosome” for each of them. The node_id column is a low-level numerical identifier for such chromosome used by the underlying tskit Python module which handles tree-sequence operations.
Here are both columns for the couple of individuals separately, making it clear that there are always two entries for each of them:

tracts %>% group_by(name)  %>% filter(name == "popY_71") %>% distinct(haplotype, node_id)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
# Groups:   name [1]
  name    haplotype node_id
  <chr>       <int>   <dbl>
1 popY_71         1     160
2 popY_71         2     161

tracts %>% group_by(name)  %>% filter(name == "popY_80") %>% distinct(haplotype, node_id)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
# Groups:   name [1]
  name    haplotype node_id
  <chr>       <int>   <dbl>
1 popY_80         1     178
2 popY_80         2     179






In the script above, I provided the function plot_tracts() for you. The way it works is that you give it a table of all tracts and the names of some individuals recorded in the tree sequence.
You can probably guess what this function does. To test this function, give it the simulated tracts data frame and a vector of names of individuals who span a wider range of “aDNA time points”, starting from the oldest individual and ending by an individual “from the present day” (but no more than one individual from each time point, just to keep things manageable).
What do you see in terms of the number of tracts and the length of tracts across these individuals? Can you detect some distinctive pattern or differences between the individual tracts (even just visually, we’ll do this more rigorously later)?






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s apply some tidyverse table munging to select individuals of different times(remember, we recorded oldest individuals at 1000 generations ago, the youngest individuals at 0 generations ago). Of course, you could also do this manually, but this is more effective, particularly if we needed to subsample many individuals.

names <- tracts %>% group_by(time) %>% distinct(name) %>% slice_sample(n = 1) %>% pull(name)
names

[1] "popY_80" "popY_66" "popY_54"


We then simply provide these names to the helper function:

plot_tracts(tracts, names)








It looks like the older individual is, the closer they lived to the start of the admixture event, and the longer the tracts they carry will be. Which makes perfect sense!




If we were interested in benchmarking some inference methods (all of which produce data very similar to the tracts table), this is the ground truth we would be comparing its performance against—effectively the results of “the perfect method” which never makes a mistake.
We’ll give a tip on how to do this benchmarking in practice in the final exercise of this chapter.

title: Haplotype-based methods
text:
Exercise: Dating admixture events
Once we have a set of admixture tracts (either simulated or inferred empirically), we can try to date the admixture event. Again, we simulated our tracts and so we know this admixture date exactly, of course. But that’s not the point here. Typically what we want to do is to simulate genomic data (see the final exercise) from our model, and then use this data as an input to external inference software to ask the question: How well can this software infer the truth? An example of such software is DATES, MOSAIC, or FLARE.
Still, let’s do a little theoretical exercise to demonstrate how admixture tract coordinates can be used to infer admixture times. In fact, this is not far from how the methods mentioned above actually do this, so it’s quite useful to know even besides intellectual curiosity.

First, compute the average length of a ancestry tracts in individuals recorded in each time point, then visualize the length distribution of these tracts stratified by their length (i.e., assign a color to each distribution).
Hint: You only need a little bit of tidyverse and ggplot2 knowledge to do this. Take a look at the relevant chapters on the left if you need a refresher. We did something similar with our example IBD data set.






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s compute the average length in each time bin:

tracts %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(mean(length))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
   time `mean(length)`
  <dbl>          <dbl>
1     0        247912.
2   200        398617.
3   400       1153801.


Obviously, we can see that the older the individual, the closer to the admixture event that individual is and, consequently, the longer the admixture tracts are. This is, of course, because recombination hadn’t yet had the time to break up longer admixture chunks into shorter pieces.
We can get a better idea about this by plotting the admixture tract length distributions like this:

ggplot(tracts, aes(length, color = factor(time))) +
  geom_density() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 3e6)) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_discrete("Time of\nrecording") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of admixture lengths, stratified by age group",
       x = "admixture tract length [bp]")












Suppose we only have sequences of present-day individuals. In our script, let’s subset the tracts data frame to only individuals recorded at time 0 (“the present day”):

tracts <- filter(tracts, time == 0)


When we look again at the distribution of tracts lengths observed in individuals at time 0 a bit more carefully, we can notice that it seems to follow the exponential distribution:









Exponential distribution is governed by the following density function with a rate parameter \(\lambda\):
\[
f(\textrm{tract length }~x) \sim \lambda \exp^{-\lambda x}
\]
In the case of exponential decay of admixture tracts and after making some simplifying assumptions, the \(\lambda\) rate parameter can be parametrized as:
\[ \lambda = \frac{1}{r t}, \] where \(r\) is the recombination rate and \(t\) is the time (in generations) since the admixture event.
The expected value of such exponential distribution is given by:
\[
\mathop{\mathbb{E}} [X] = \frac{1}{\lambda}
\]
Because we can get the maximum likelihood value of this expected average simply by computing a simple mean of tract lengths \(\bar{x}\), we can also write:
\[
\bar{x} \approx \mathop{\mathbb{E}} [X] = \frac{1}{\lambda}.
\]
Simply by rearranging this equation, we can therefore get an estimate the rate of exponential decay \(\hat{\lambda}\) of the underlying exponential distribution of the tract lengths as:
\[
\hat{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\bar{x}}.
\]
We can also verify our assumptions by overlaying a theoretical exponential distribution density corresponding to the tract length data. (This is a very technical bit, so feel free to skip this):






NoteClick to see the solution





We can do this using the dexp() function:












But more importantly, because we know that \(\lambda = 1 / (r t)\), assuming we know the uniform average recombination rate \(r\) reasonably well, we can estimate the time of admixture simply by rearranging this equation to extract the admixture time \(t\) as:
\[
t \approx \frac{\hat{\lambda}}{r}
\]
For example, given a vector of tract lengths in our simulated individuals “from the present day”:

head(tracts$length, 10) # ... etc

 [1] 171668  16025 413619  97932  87025 807168  48615  96072  33498  77603


we can estimate the rate of exponential decay \(\hat{\lambda}\) like this:

lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(tracts$length)
lambda_hat

[1] 4.033696e-06


and then use this value to estimate of time since admixture in the history of these individual directly:

r <- 1e-8 # recombination rate (crossovers per bp per generation)

admixture_time <- lambda_hat / r # admixture time in "generations before this individual lived"

admixture_time

[1] 403.3696



You can see that we’re a little bit of from the true value of 500 generations (after all, we only simulated a small part of the genome), but still, hopefully this gives you a hint of how admixture dating methods work, at least in principle.
Real-world inference uses mathematical machinery which is a little bit more sophisticated (usually we deal with filtered tracts, or we don’t even have full haplotypes and can only work with linkage information between individual alleles), but the general ideas remains the same—fitting an exponential curve to the information signal left in admixed genomes by the process of recombination.

title: Haplotype-based methods
text:
Exercise: Identity-by-Descent segments (IBD)
Another function useful for studying demographic history using haplotypes is ts_ibd(). As the name suggests, this function extracts IBD segments for the given set of individuals recorded in a tree sequence.
Let’s first get the names of individuals “at the present”:

samples <- ts_recorded(ts) %>% filter(time == 0)
samples

# A tibble: 30 × 3
   name     time pop  
   <chr>   <dbl> <chr>
 1 popX_1      0 popX 
 2 popX_2      0 popX 
 3 popX_3      0 popX 
 4 popX_4      0 popX 
 5 popX_5      0 popX 
 6 popX_6      0 popX 
 7 popX_7      0 popX 
 8 popX_8      0 popX 
 9 popX_9      0 popX 
10 popX_10     0 popX 
# ℹ 20 more rows


In general, there are two modes of operation for the ts_ibd() function (depending on whether we set its argument within or between) as outlined bellow.
(Additionally, because the IBD data from even a tiny simulation can be absolutely huge, we typically need to pre-filter which IBDs to extract, for instance by setting the maximum_time argument, which only searches for IBDs that aren’t resulting from a most recent common ancestor (MRCA) not older than the given time. Alternatively, we also have the option to filter for minimum_length, but see the instructions in ?ts_ibd for some caveats.)

We can look for IBD segments within a given group of individuals by providing the names of the group of individuals within which to extract IBD segments.


ibd_within <- ts_ibd(ts, within = samples$name, maximum_time = 100)

Looking at the data, we see a familiar data frame structure again, namely with pairs of names of two individuals name1 and name2 for each IBD segment (each row of the data frame), the time tmrca of the most common ancestor from which the IBD segment was inherited.
When we summarize how many segments of what average length do we find in our simulated sample set (a simple metric of relatedness), we can see that the amount of IBDs follows the \(N_e\) of the population in our model: the smaller the \(N_e\), the more related (and with more IBD) we observe in our populations:

ibd_within %>%
  group_by(pop1, pop2) %>%
  summarize(ibd_count = n(), ibd_length = mean(length))

# A tibble: 3 × 4
# Groups:   pop1 [3]
  pop1  pop2  ibd_count ibd_length
  <fct> <fct>     <int>      <dbl>
1 popZ  popZ       1540   1112047.
2 popX  popX        513   1325700.
3 popY  popY         92    965703.



plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)









We can look for IBD segments between two groups by providing two sets of individuals.

Let’s first convert our present-day only table of samples into the necessary format (list of vectors, as we discussed many times before).

samples <- split(samples$name, samples$pop)
samples

$popX
 [1] "popX_1"  "popX_2"  "popX_3"  "popX_4"  "popX_5"  "popX_6"  "popX_7" 
 [8] "popX_8"  "popX_9"  "popX_10"

$popY
 [1] "popY_71" "popY_72" "popY_73" "popY_74" "popY_75" "popY_76" "popY_77"
 [8] "popY_78" "popY_79" "popY_80"

$popZ
 [1] "popZ_1"  "popZ_2"  "popZ_3"  "popZ_4"  "popZ_5"  "popZ_6"  "popZ_7" 
 [8] "popZ_8"  "popZ_9"  "popZ_10"


Let’s run ts_ibd() with the between mode. Notice that we see nothing between any pair of the three populations if we keep the maximum_time = 100 filter present. This makes sense because the splits between the populations (and their \(N_e\)) don’t allow for such “young” IBD segments to persist. This applies also to the popY-popX pair whose demographic history involves a substantial gene flow event of 20%!

ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popZ", "popX")], maximum_time = 100)

[1] node1 node2 mrca  tmrca left  right
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popZ", "popY")], maximum_time = 100)

[1] node1 node2 mrca  tmrca left  right
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popY", "popX")], maximum_time = 100)

[1] node1 node2 mrca  tmrca left  right
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)


We see the same thing between the popY-popX pair even when we filter for IBD segments inherited right at the time the gene-flow ended (obviously):

ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popY", "popX")], maximum_time = 499)

[1] node1 node2 mrca  tmrca left  right
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)


Finally, we do pick up an admixture signal when we allow IBD segments tracing the MRCA between the two populations to the exact generation during which the admixture began:

ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popY", "popX")], maximum_time = 500)

# A tibble: 10 × 13
   node1 node2 length  mrca node1_time node2_time tmrca     left    right name1 
   <int> <int>  <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <chr> 
 1   142   178 156916  7917          0          0  499. 54401344 54558260 popX_2
 2   144   172  25925  7931          0          0  500. 53903357 53929282 popX_3
 3   144   178 243159  7917          0          0  499. 54315101 54558260 popX_3
 4   145   172  25925  7931          0          0  500. 53903357 53929282 popX_3
 5   145   178   8468  7917          0          0  499. 54524139 54532607 popX_3
 6   148   178 138802  7917          0          0  499. 54315101 54453903 popX_5
 7   150   178  83307  7917          0          0  499. 54412132 54495439 popX_6
 8   151   178 138802  7917          0          0  499. 54315101 54453903 popX_6
 9   156   178 138802  7917          0          0  499. 54315101 54453903 popX_9
10   158   178 138802  7917          0          0  499. 54315101 54453903 popX_…
# ℹ 3 more variables: name2 <chr>, pop1 <fct>, pop2 <fct>



Unlike every single statistical method introduced in this workshop, there’s a caveat to using ts_ibd() used for real-world simulation-based inference of demographic history or software benchmarking, and it has to do with an issue in how the underlying tskit tree-sequence machinery handles IBD segments. Read the linked GitHub issue as well as my note in the ?ts_ibd help page to learn more.
That said, if you want to do real-world inference using IBD segments on real data, this would anyway require applying third-party software doing the inference anyway (AncIBD, IBDSeq, Ibis, etc.). For this reason, this issue doesn’t have much practical implication.
For those applications, let’s move on to how you’d go about approaching tying slendr simulations with external software.

title: Haplotype-based methods
section: Bonus exercise: Converting tree sequences to other genotype formats
text:
Bonus exercise: Converting tree sequences to other genotype formats
As convenient as it is to always work in R with user-friendly modeling interface of slendr, it’s library of tskit tree-sequence statistical functions, and the whole tidyverse and ggplot2 data science packages, real-world research requires using third-party external software. In general, software like this doesn’t work with tree-sequence data structures, and even when it does, our real-world data doesn’t come in the form of tree sequences—it takes the form of genotype files such as VCF, EIGENSTRAT, PLINK, and others.
Luckily, slendr provides convenient means to convert tree sequences into standard genotype formats. For instance, if we have a tree sequence object ts, we can:

Obtain a VCF file with the function ts_vcf()


ts_vcf(ts, path = "/tmp/genotypes.vcf.gz")


bcftools view -s popX_1,popY_1,popZ_1 /tmp/genotypes.vcf.gz | head -n15
