#   popY_10_chr2 <int>, popY_11_chr1 <int>, popY_11_chr2 <int>,
#   popY_12_chr1 <int>, popY_12_chr2 <int>, popY_13_chr1 <int>, …



With these three functions, you can always finish your slendr simulation scripts with a file conversion to another fileformat and pick up your inference work in a different third-party software (IBDseq, DATES, ADMIXTOOLS, PLINK, etc.).

title: Overview of projects
text:
You have now learned nearly everything there is to know about technical aspects of slendr modeling and seen many different examples of various techniques to apply simulations in your own work. All that remains now is for you to gain your own experience through practice.
Here is a selection of small projects representing case studies from various contexts of population genetics, many of which should be immediately applicable in your own work (certainly the simulation and computational techniques will be, if not the exact same statistics). There are also a couple of opportunities for practicing on problems which are more in line with the exercises we went through until this point, just in case you still feel a little uncertain about programming simulations. On the opposite side of the spectrum, there are also suggestions for much more open-ended and more ambitious project ideas, in case you feel like having an extra challenge!

title: AFS-based inference of \(N_e\)
text:
Part 1: A self-contained data-generating slendr function
Imagine you sequenced 1 Mb of sequence of ten individuals from a population of your interest and computed a summary statistic such as the allele frequency spectrum (AFS). Those sequences (and, by extension, the AFS) were produced by a real-world biological process (demographic history) which is hidden but which you want to learn about. Prior bioinformatic studies estimated that the recombination and mutation rates of this population are both 1e-8 (just like in humans).
Now you want to use this data to estimate the population’s long-term \(N_e\) which is, of course, unknown (you only have the observed AFS). Suppose that the only thing known about the population size from some other hypothetical evidence that this \(N_e\) was somewhere between 1000 and 30000.
(\(N_e\) is just an example here—in practice, we’re typically interested in other parameters as well (admixture rate, admixture time, split times, etc.), but the idea remains the same: we computed summaries of the empirical data which were shaped by those hidden parameters and we need to estimate them.)
Simulations can be a great tool to estimate the most likely value of such an unknown parameters. In this exercise, you’re going to simulate a large number of AFS vectors (each resulting from a different assumed \(N_e\) value) and then pick just those \(N_e\) values (or just one \(N_e\) value) which produced a simulated AFS closest to the observed AFS. This is the core idea behind simulation-based inference and applies to many other situations and modeling contexts.
To make things manageable, let’s decompose the problem into a sequence of steps.
Create a new script inference_afs.R. In this script, program a function called simulate_afs(), which will take Ne as its only parameter and will contain a single-population slendr demographic model. In this function, use ts_afs() to compute (and return) the AFS vector on a sample of 10 individuals in the tree sequence produced by this model. When you return the AFS vector from this function, make sure to drop the first and last elements (with something like afs[-c(1, 21)]). Test this function on a couple of Ne values of your choosing, but staying between Ne = 1000 and Ne = 30000 and plot them to observe how (and why) do they differ based on Ne parameter you used in each respective simulation. If you want more information about AFS, see the help page under ?ts_afs.
Hint: If you need help, take a look at the exercise chapter which introduced the concepts of slendr model functions generating some statistics, or feel free to start building your inference_afs.R solution based on the following “template” (just fill in missing relevant bits of slendr code that you should be already familiar with).
When used in R, your custom function should work like this (the simulation is stochastic, so your numbers will be different, of course):
In summary, your function should give you a vector of singletons, doubletons, etc., all the way to the number of fixed mutations in our sample of 10 individuals, looking something like this:
simulate_afs(Ne = 1000)

 [1] 428 191 111  94  73  54  49  50  63  50  31  53  22  17  19  24  23  16  15

title: AFS-based inference of \(N_e\)
text:
Note: If you want to know why I asked you to drop the first and last element of the ts_afs() output (for instance with something like afs[-c(1, 20)]), it’s due to technical reasons related to how the underlying tskit module operates. You don’t have to worry about that here, but you can read this for more detail.






NoteClick to see the “template”






library(slendr)
init_env()

simulate_afs <- function(Ne) {
  # In here you should write code which will:
  #   1. create one population with a given Ne (provided as a function argument)
  #   2. compile the model (either forward-time or backward-time, doesn't matter)
  #   3. simulate a tree sequence
  #   4. select a subset of 10 individuals (you could also schedule ther recording)
  #   5. compute AFS vector from those 10 individuals using `ts_afs()`
  
  # `result` is a variable with your 10-sample AFS vector (we remove the
  # first and last element because it's not meaningful for our example)
  return(result[-c(1, 21)]) 
}

# test the function on a few example runs
afs1k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 1000)
plot(afs1k, type ="o")

afs7k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 7000)
plot(afs7k, type ="o")


















NoteClick to see the solution





The point of the exercise is for you to force yourself to push through the frustration. These case studies were designed to put you in a situation in which you have to address a research problem without a known solution and let you practice this in a safe environment. Please, only take a look at the solution if you’re either done with your own code, or if you want to compare your solution to mine:






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the complete script inference_afs.R so far:

library(slendr)
init_env()

simulate_afs <- function(Ne) {
  # create a slendr model with a single population of size Ne = N
  pop <- population("pop", N = Ne, time = 1000)
  model <- compile_model(pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(pop, 10))

  # simulate a tree sequence
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # get the names of the 10 individuals in the tree sequence
  samples <- ts_names(ts)

  # compute the AFS vector
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(samples))

  # return the AFS (without the first and last element)
  return(afs[-c(1, length(afs))])
}

Our function is supposed to produce an AFS vector of counts of alleles observed at a given frequency in the population sample. Let’s verify that our custom function works correctly by simulating an AFS vector for Ne = 1k, 10k, and 30k:

afs_1k <- simulate_afs(1000)
afs_10k <- simulate_afs(10000)
afs_30k <- simulate_afs(30000)

Here’s one of those vectors. We can see that the function does, indeed, produce a result of the correct format:

afs_1k

 [1] 393 170 160 106  94  64  67  41  35  23  24  39  31  34  44  19  19  19  10


To see the results of this function in a clearer context, let’s visualize the vectors in the same plot:

plot(afs_30k, type = "o", main = "AFS, Ne = 30000", col = "cyan", ylim = c(0, max(afs_30k)))
lines(afs_10k, type = "o", main = "AFS, Ne = 10000", col = "purple")
lines(afs_1k, type = "o", main = "AFS, Ne = 1000", col = "blue")
legend("topright", legend = c("Ne = 1k", "Ne = 10k", "Ne = 30k"),
       fill = c("blue", "purple", "cyan"))

title: AFS-based inference of \(N_e\)
section: Part 2: Matching simulated AFS against empirical AFS
text:
Part 2: Matching simulated AFS against empirical AFS
This is the empirical AFS you computed from the 10 sequenced genomes of your individuals of interest (perhaps with software like PLINK):

afs_observed <- c(2493, 1167, 876, 649, 539, 543, 381, 330, 338, 211,
                  268, 183, 205, 214, 155, 176, 144, 122, 121)

Now use your slendr function simulate_afs() and a few other techniques you learned throughout this workshop to “guess” the true (but hidden) \(N_e\) of your population of interest, given this observed AFS. Depending on how confident you feel with coding, there are two possible options:

Option 1 [easy but not rigorous]: Plot AFS vectors simulated for various \(N_e\) values, then try to guess (just by looking at the AFS visualizations) which one looks closest to the empirical AFS and, therefore, which simulated \(N_e\) is the closest match to the reality. (This is, of course, not how proper statistical inference is done, but it’s a good start if you’re just starting with simulation-based inference.)
Option 2 [harder and more rigorous]: Simulate AFS vectors across a grid of possible Ne values depending on your prior information (perhaps using base R lapply() or purrr map()), and find the \(N_e\) which results in a simulated AFS which is closest to the observed AFS by computing Mean squared error on the two of them.







NoteClick to see the solution to “Option 1”





This is the empirical AFS to which we need to compare our simulated AFS vectors:

afs_observed <- c(2493, 1167, 876, 649, 539, 543, 381, 330, 338, 211,
                  268, 183, 205, 214, 155, 176, 144, 122, 121)

We know that the true \(N_e\) is supposed to be between 1000 and 30000, so let’s simulate a couple of AFS vectors for different \(N_e\) values using our new AFS simulation function:

afs_Ne1k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 1000)
afs_Ne5k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 5000)
afs_Ne6k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 6000)
afs_Ne10k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 10000)
afs_Ne20k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 20000)
afs_Ne30k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 30000)

Now let’s plot our simulated AFS vectors together with the observed AFS (shown in black):

plot(afs_observed, type = "b", col = "black", lwd = 3,
     xlab = "allele count bin", ylab = "count", ylim = c(0, 13000))
lines(afs_Ne1k, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
lines(afs_Ne5k, lwd = 2, col = "green")
lines(afs_Ne6k, lwd = 2, col = "pink")
lines(afs_Ne10k, lwd = 2, col = "purple")
lines(afs_Ne20k, lwd = 2, col = "orange")
lines(afs_Ne30k, lwd = 2, col = "cyan")
legend("topright",
       legend = c("observed AFS", "Ne = 1000", "Ne = 5000",
                  "Ne = 6000", "Ne = 10000", "Ne = 20000", "Ne = 30000"),
       fill = c("black", "blue", "green", "pink", "purple", "orange", "cyan"))








From the figure, we can see that the black line (empirical AFS) seems to be closest to the simulated \(N_e\) = 6000.
And indeed, I can now reveal that the true \(N_e\) of our population of interest was 6543. Not a bad result for such a simple inference pipeline!

Having done the “Option 1” solution, now consider taking a stab at the “Option 2”. It’s not that much harder, actually, and you’ve already practiced everything you need to solve this. You’ve got this!









NoteClick to see the solution to “Option 2”





This is the empirical AFS to which we need to compare our simulated AFS vectors:

afs_observed <- c(2493, 1167, 876, 649, 539, 543, 381, 330, 338, 211,
                  268, 183, 205, 214, 155, 176, 144, 122, 121)

We know that the true \(N_e\) is supposed to be between 1000 and 30000. Let’s generate a regular grid of potential \(N_e\) values for which we want to simulate AFS vectors:

Ne_grid <- seq(from = 1000, to = 30000, by = 500)
Ne_grid

 [1]  1000  1500  2000  2500  3000  3500  4000  4500  5000  5500  6000  6500
[13]  7000  7500  8000  8500  9000  9500 10000 10500 11000 11500 12000 12500
[25] 13000 13500 14000 14500 15000 15500 16000 16500 17000 17500 18000 18500
[37] 19000 19500 20000 20500 21000 21500 22000 22500 23000 23500 24000 24500
[49] 25000 25500 26000 26500 27000 27500 28000 28500 29000 29500 30000


With the parameter grid Ne_grid set up, let’s simulate an AFS from each \(N_e\) model (we simply loop over the grid using a parallel version of lapply() to speed things up, but plain lapply() or map() would work too):

library(parallel)

afs_grid <- mclapply(Ne_grid, simulate_afs, mc.cores = detectCores() - 1)
names(afs_grid) <- Ne_grid

Here’s an example of the first five simulated AFS vectors, just to demonstrate what the output of the grid simulations looks like. As you can see, we get a list of numerical vectors, one element of the list corresponding to one AFS (and indexed by the corresponding Ne):

afs_grid[1:5]

$`1000`
 [1] 446 167 138 101  79  77  64  43  44  37  39  33  35  22  14  23  20   9  12

$`1500`
 [1] 640 383 200 147 126  92  88 102  94  76  57  67  48  30  45  27  30  32  28

$`2000`
 [1] 790 406 257 252 150 191 139 116  93  84  77  68  67  78  56  65  53  26  38

$`2500`
 [1] 981 499 358 276 230 198 178 151  99  93  87  73  64  91  83  64  52  38  42

$`3000`
 [1] 1266  624  331  297  246  205  145  136  155   98  114   89   90   68   65
[16]   67   72   65   73


To get a better idea of the grid simulations, let’s visualize the observed AFS (in black) and overlay the simulated AFS vectors on top of it (in gray):

# plot the observed AFS in black
plot(afs_observed, type = "b", col = "black", lwd = 3, xlab = "allele count bin", ylab = "count")

# then loop over the list with simulated AFS, overlaying them onto the plot
for (i in seq_along(Ne_grid)) {
  lines(afs_grid[[i]], lwd = 0.5)
}

# add a legend too
legend("topright", legend = c("observed AFS", "simulated AFS"), fill = c("black", "gray"))








Instead of just eyeballing the closest AFS like we do in “Option 1” (which is impossible to do here anyway because of how many AFS vectors we simulated), we want to compute the mean squared error of the AFS produced by each \(N_e\) value across the grid:

# loop over simulated AFS vectors and compute the MSE from the observed AFS for each
error_grid <- sapply(afs_grid, function(afs_simulated) {
  sum((afs_simulated - afs_observed)^2) / length(afs_simulated)
})

Let’s visualize the error of each simulated AFS and highlight the one which was closest to the empirical AFS:

plot(Ne_grid, error_grid, ylab = "error")

abline(v = Ne_grid[which.min(error_grid)], col = "red")

legend("topright", legend = paste("minimum error Ne =", Ne_grid[which.min(error_grid)]), fill = "red")








Plot the AFS again, but this time highlight the AFS which is the most statistically likely (i.e. the one which gave the lowest MSE value):

# plot the observed AFS again
plot(afs_observed, type = "b", col = "black", lwd = 3, xlab = "allele count bin", ylab = "count")

# loop over each simulated AFS...
for (i in seq_along(Ne_grid)) {
  # ... and assign a red color to the one which was the closest based on
  # the computed error from the observed AFS
  color <- if (i == which.min(error_grid)) "red" else "gray"
  width <- if (i == which.min(error_grid)) 2 else 0.75

  lines(afs_grid[[i]], lwd = width, col = color)
}

legend("topright", legend = c("observed AFS", paste("best fitting Ne =", Ne_grid[which.min(error_grid)])),
       fill = c("black", "red"))








The true \(N_e\) was 6543, which fits our inference result very well!




Congratulations, you now know how to infer parameters of evolutionary models using simulations! What you just did is really very similar to how simulation-based inference is done in practice (even with methods such as ABC). Hopefully you now also see how easy slendr makes it to do this process.
As mentioned in the introduction, this kind of approach can be used to infer all sorts of demographic parameters using simulation-based inference, even using other summary statistics that you’ve also learned to compute (\(f\)-statistics, nucleotide diversity, IBD data, etc.).

title: Comparing \(f_3\) versus \(f_4\)
text:
Suppose you want to test for evidence of admixture in some population of interest assuming some demographic model (we’re talking general case here, think of any model you’d like). In our exercises earlier, we’ve seen that both \(f_3\) and \(f_4\) can be used for this purpose—in fact, they were both originally developed as admixture tests. What’s more, they’re both used in the literature for for this purpose in practical research.
Imagine you need to convince a reviewer that one or the other statistic is better for your application, or you need to pick an appropriate statistic to test for evidence of admixture a study you’re currently working on and want to justify your decision using simulations based on the specifics of your assumed model (after all, all of our inferences are based on some assumptions).
Build a simulation pipeline using the slendr modeling building blocks and the simulation techniques you’ve learned in this workshop and find answers to questions such as:

Under which conditions would the \(f_3\) or \(f_4\) be more applicable as an admixture test? Is one of them more suitable for some particular kind of model or some specific model parameters than the other? Proportion of admixture? Time of admixture? Effective population size?
Is one perhaps more noisy than the other? Is one more sensitive to detect evidence of admixture in some situation (but perhaps not in another situation)?

My suggestion is to start with a baseline model which is as simple as possible and generalize it into a function with parameters whose effect you’d like to investigate—perhaps one of the general four-population demographic models from our \(f\)-statistic explorations would make a good starting point.

title: Neanderthal ancestry trajectory
text:
Preparation
In this case study, you will be reproducing an important result from my 2018 study on the limits of selection against Neanderthal introgression. In a very unplanned and unpredictable manner, this research ended up turning into a study on the importance of model assumptions on the robustness of inferences with \(f_4\) statistics and how they can produce entirely misleading inferences about ancient admixture events in human history.
I chose this case study for several reasons:
To avoid too much frustration with transcribing very complex admixture graph model from yet another of my drawings, please copy the following code into a new script introgression.R. When you visualize the model, you should see a relatively detailed (yet still simplified) model of ancient human history including Neanderthal introgression into the ancestors of non-Africans. Again, please inspect this script to make sure you understand what it does—this is now even more important than before.
Please note that real-world simulations are rather computationally intensive, much more so than the modeling we did in our exercises. Generally speaking, most of simulation-based research happens on big computational servers. For our learning purposes here, if things take too long, just lower the amount of simulated sequence. However, be aware that this will, in turn, make statistics much more noisy (but that’s OK, we’re learning here).

title: Neanderthal ancestry trajectory
text:
NoteClick to see the the script introgression.R






library(slendr)
init_env()

outgroup <- population("outgroup",   time = 7000000, N = 10000)

ancestor <- population("ancestor",   time = 6000001, N =  1000, parent = outgroup, remove = 599999)

altai    <- population("Altai",      time =  600000, N =  1000, parent = ancestor, remove = 49999)
vindija  <- population("Vindija",    time =  200000, N =  1000, parent = altai, remove = 49999)

san      <- population("San",        time =  600000, N = 10000, parent = ancestor)
mbuti    <- population("Mbuti",      time =  350000, N = 10000, parent = san)
yoruba   <- population("Yoruba",     time =  220000, N = 10000, parent = mbuti)
dinka    <- population("Dinka",      time =  150000, N = 15000, parent = yoruba)

nonafr   <- population("nonAfrican", time =   70000, N = 3000,  parent = dinka)

gf <- gene_flow(from = vindija, to = nonafr, proportion = 0.03, start = 55000, end = 50000)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, ancestor, altai, vindija, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  gene_flow = gf,
  generation_time = 30
)

# schedule recording of present-day individuals
schedule_present <- schedule_recording(
  model, times = 0,
  list(outgroup, 1), list(san, 1), list(mbuti, 1), list(yoruba, 1), list(dinka, 1), list(nonafr, 1)
)

# schedule recording of two Nenderthals
schedule_neand <- schedule_recording(model, times = 50000, list(altai, 1, "Altai"), list(vindija, 1, "Vindija"))

# schedule recording of Upper-Paleolithic modern humans
schedule_emh <- schedule_recording(model, times = runif(n = 50, min = 1000, max = 45000), list(nonafr, 1))

# bind the schedules into one
schedule <- rbind(schedule_present, schedule_neand, schedule_emh)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 100e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

In case your simulation takes too long or your computer seems to be struggling, you can replace your tree-sequence simulation command by this bit of code which reads my simulated ts object from the internet. Then, continue working with it as if you had simulated it yourself.






NoteClick to see the download command






ts_path <- tempfile()
options(timeout = 600)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodkan/simgen/refs/heads/main/files/introgression/base_409046.trees", destfile = ts_path, mode = "wb")
ts <- ts_read(file = ts_path, model = model)




Here’s the model visualization (very janky, I know, but it is what it is…):

cowplot::plot_grid(
  plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule),
  plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule, log = TRUE),
  ncol = 2
)

title: Neanderthal ancestry trajectory
text:
Indirect \(f_4\)-ratio estimate of Neanderthal ancestry
The main controversy at the time I did this research was caused by the observation that ancient DNA time series of early modern humans (like the one you just simulated!) showed a clear decline in Neanderthal ancestry trajectory over the past ~45 thousand years.
The way the authors of the “Neanderthal decline” paper computed Neanderthal ancestry was using what I ended up naming as the “indirect \(f_4\)-ratio” estimate, described in panel B of Figure 1 in my paper (where “Dinka” typically represented the “East African” lineage, and “Yoruba” represented the “Central and West African” lineage, to follow the terminology in that schematic diagram). This “indirect” estimate is what showed clear evidence of the decline in Neanderthal ancestry over time.

Compute this “indirect \(f_4\)-ratio” estimate of Neanderthal ancestry from your simulated ts tree sequence for every one of your “nonAfrican” individuals. Then visualize the simulated Neanderthal ancestry trajectory as a time-series (i.e., your indirect ancestry estimate on the y-axis, time on the x-axis), similarly to what’s shown for the empirical data linked above. What kind of temporal trend do you observe?
Hint: You can either compute this “manually” using the path overlap principles described in the \(f\) statistics chapter earlier, or you can make your life a bit easier and use a dedicated slendr function ts_f4ratio(). That function follows the same nomenclature shown in my Figure 1B diagram above. If you use ts_f4ratio(), be aware that X can only always be one individual in this function, so you will want to compute this for every aDNA individual in the time-series separately.
Hint: If you need more help, see this example of how to compute the indirect \(f_4\)-ratio for a single individual.






NoteClick to see the hint





Here’s a manual calculation of the “indirect \(f_4\)-ratio” as a ratio of two \(f_4\) statistics for a single individual “nonAfrican_1”:

ts_f4(ts, W = s["Yoruba"], X = s["outgroup"], Y = "nonAfrican_1", Z = "Vindija")$f4 /
ts_f4(ts, W = s["Yoruba"], X = s["outgroup"], Y = s["Dinka"], Z = "Vindija")$f4

[1] 0.9781058


Here’s how the function ts_f4ratio() can be used for the same purpose:

ts_f4ratio(ts, X = "nonAfrican_1", A = s["Yoruba"], B = s["Dinka"], C = "Altai", O = s["outgroup"])

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  X            A      B     C     O        statistic                       alpha
  <chr>        <chr>  <chr> <chr> <chr>    <chr>                           <dbl>
1 nonAfrican_1 Yoruba Dinka Altai outgroup f4-ratio(nonAfrican_1;Yoruba,D… 0.978


Note, however, that this estimate effectively infers the “modern human ancestry” represented by our shared genetic roots in Africa. To arrive to a Neanderthal ancestry estimate, we need to compute it’s complement:

1 - ts_f4ratio(ts, X = "nonAfrican_1", A = s["Yoruba"], B = s["Dinka"], C = "Altai", O = s["outgroup"])$alpha

[1] 0.02191806


This is close to our simulated 3% Neanderthal ancestry proportion, which is reassuring!









NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s what my simulated trajectory looks like:

title: Neanderthal ancestry trajectory
section: Adding complex admixture during modern human prehistory
text:
Adding complex admixture during modern human prehistory
In your visualization of the indirect \(f_4\)-ratio trajectory, you should have noticed no trend at all. Indeed, under neutrality, Neanderthal ancestry is expected to constant throughout the millenia. However, the puzzle at the time was that the empirical data showed clear, significant temporal decline in this estimate over time!
The solution to the puzzle came out of (lots of) simulations and modeling, very similar to what you’ve done in this workshop so far. Let’s retrace my steps again.

What happens if you introduce additional gene flow events within the modern human population tree? For example, simulate admixture between the two African lineages used in your indirect \(f_4\)-ratio calculation, as well as “back-flow” admixture from the non-African population into both of those African lineages. Let’s say that all of these admixture events should happen at 5% proportion, the within-Africa gene flow should happen starting from 20 kya until present-day time 0, and the backflow nonAfrican admixture should happen from 8 kya to 5 kya.
None of those changes into the demographic model changes the amount of true Neanderthal ancestry in Europeans. But what does the trajectory of the indirect Neanderthal ancestry estimate look like when you compute it on this model with additional complex admixture within modern humans?
Hint: Feel free to make a copy of your introgression.R script to make the indicated changes, perhaps saving it as introgression_complex.R, just to make things clean and tidy.
Again, if you think your tree-sequence simulation takes too long or that your computer is struggling, feel free to use this chunk of code to read my own ts tree sequence from the internet, then continue working with it as if you simulated it yourself:






NoteClick to see the download command






ts_path <- tempfile()
options(timeout = 600)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodkan/simgen/refs/heads/main/files/introgression/admix_725458.trees", destfile = ts_path, mode = "wb")
ts <- ts_read(file = ts_path, model = model)










NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s what my simulated trajectory looks like on the modified model:









We pick up a decline in Neanderthal ancestry even though we know there’s no decline at all! This is because the indirect \(f_4\)-ratio make very strong assumptions about the population tree of modern humans, specifically the fact that there was no admixture between different modern human lineages after Neanderthal introgression.
Don’t worry if your own result is noisy! That’s what replicate simulations are for (remember the existence of the ts_replicate() function, which I wrote exactly for this purpose).

title: Neanderthal ancestry trajectory
text:
Direct \(f_4\)-ratio estimate of Neanderthal ancestry
The reason we had to compute Neanderthal ancestry using the “indirect” statistic is because we only had a single Neanderthal genome available at the time—the genome of the “Altai” Neanderthal.
Luckily, a few years later, a second Neanderthal was sequenced which allowed us to express the \(f_4\)-ratio estimate in a “direct” way using both Neanderthal genomes. We called this estimate the “direct \(f_4\)-ratio” estimate.
If you got to the relevant part of the \(f\)-statistics chapter, you may remember that we discovered multiple ways of computing the px ancestry—either coming from the p3 population (we could call it alpha), or as its complement coming from the p2 population (we could compute it as 1 - alpha). Well, the “indirect vs direct \(f_4\)-ratio” situation is exactly the same.
Using this idea, compute the “direct \(f_4\)-ratio” using the two Neanderthal genomes on the model which includes lots of complex admixture within modern humans. How does the direct \(f_4\)-ratio perform on such a model? Is it robust and can it infer the Neanderthal ancestry trajectory accurately, unlike the indirect estimate?
Hint: If you need help, see this example of how to compute the direct \(f_4\)-ratio for a single individual again.






NoteClick to see the hint





Here’s how the function ts_f4ratio() can be used for this calculation. Basically, we exchange the two African lineages for the two Neanderthal lineages, it’s as simple as that:

ts_f4ratio(ts, X = "nonAfrican_1", A = "Altai", B = "Vindija", C = s["Dinka"], O = s["outgroup"])

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  X            A     B       C     O        statistic                      alpha
  <chr>        <chr> <chr>   <chr> <chr>    <chr>                          <dbl>
1 nonAfrican_1 Altai Vindija Dinka outgroup f4-ratio(nonAfrican_1;Altai,… 0.0136











NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s what my simulated trajectory looks like on the modified model:









Don’t worry if your own result is noisy! That’s what replicate simulations are for (remember the existence of the ts_replicate() function, which I wrote exactly for this purpose).
Finally, here’s a comparison of both indirect and direct \(f_4\)-ratio statistics against one another. Again, bear in mind that in reality (which we know from the simulations) the proportion of Neanderthal ancestry remained the same over tens of thousands of years—but the indirect \(f_4\)-ratio statistic gives us a misleading result, because it makes assumptions about modern human population relationships which simply do not hold:


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'













In conclusion, the demographic simulation exploration in my paper took months of work (and a combination of Python simulations, shells scripts, and R data analysis scripts), resolving a problem which occupied the brightest minds of population genetics at the time. I hope that the fact that you’re able to reproduce the core aspects of this work this easily convinces you of the power of slendr modeling for this type of research!

title: Neanderthal ancestry trajectory
text:
Bonus exercise
Because I saved you a lot of work by providing the introgression admixture model already programmed, here’s a bonus challenge:
One question that the authors of the original draft Neanderthal genome paper had to answer was the issue of the direction of gene-flow.
How would you show that introgression happened from Neanderthals into non-Africans and not the other way around? Skim through the paper linked above, particularly focusing on the section called “Direction of gene flow” to get an idea of how did the authors distinguished the two scenarios using a \(D\) statistic (which, for our purposes, could be thought of as essentially equivalent to the \(f_4\) statistic as we’ve established it, so you can use the familiar \(f_4\) to answer this question).
Hint: They used logic to argue for what would the expected values of certain \(f_4\) statistics look like between two different models (the model of introgression from Neanderthals into non-Africans, and the model of introgression from non-Africans into Neanderthals). We want to use simulations to try to arrive at the same conclusions.

title: Exploring qpAdm / qpGraph models
text:
I think this particular mini project could have—out of every other case study idea on offer—the most impact on you your research in ancient DNA genomics.
Both qpAdm and qpGraph techniques form a core component of nearly every single ancient DNA paper. Yet, a lot of research work has been poured (one paper, another paper, yet another paper) into delineating in which situations qpAdm works and — much more often — when it either fails to work or when it’s often completely misinterpreted.
If you work with qpAdm, you’re aware of many assumptions and recommendations that are made, but those are rarely backed by rigorous modeling and simulation.
In this case study, I would encourage you to take some qpAdm / qpGraph models you have inferred in the past (or some foundational models inferred in the literature relevant for your work), program them in the form of a parametrized slendr model, and experiment with how robust the qpAdm conclusions are to some of the assumptions made.
Hint: You already know that slendr allows exporting data in the form of EIGENSTRAT files via the function ts_eigenstrat() (as introduced in recipes in this chapter) which means that connecting slendr simulation scripts with the ADMIXTOOLS2 software in R should be quite straightforward.

title: PCA, STRUCTURE, LAI, DATES, IBD
text:
Robustness of STRUCTURE / ADMIXTURE
Here are a couple of ideas for projects you could also work on to practice simulations and modeling. Similarly to mini projects on STRUCTURE / ADMIXTURE and ADMIXTOOLS, they are all revolving around building models to generate ground-truth data for use in:
all using external software (rather than slendr-based statistics).
Unlike the many exercises in our tutorial sessions, I can’t provide the questions for you. But, this is a workshop, and we can definitely come up with ideas to tackle these together.
STRUCTURE, ADMIXTURE, and other genetic clustering methods are extremely popular across the field of population genomics. However, it has been shown that very different models can produce exactly the same STRUCTURE / ADMIXTURE clustering patterns (see Figure 2 in that study, and an accompanying post on this paper). As a result, we have to be quite careful with the interpretation of the results.
Here are a few suggestions on what you could do in this study depending on your level of familiarity and prior experience:
crumbs: 16  PCA, STRUCTURE, LAI, DATES, IBD

title: PCA, STRUCTURE, LAI, DATES, IBD
text:
1. Have you used one of these genetic clustering methods?
Write a slendr model corresponding to the demographic history you’ve inferred, then try to experiment with its parameters or topological structure in a way following the approach the authors took in this study. How robust is your inference when you repeat it on these simulated models?


2. Are you thinking about using one of these genetic clustering methods?
Write a simulation script for each of the three model topologies in the figure linked above. Follow the methodology of the paper and try to replicate their results, including modifying the three models to convince yourself of the conclusions.


Tip: How to convert data
Note that slendr doesn’t produce PLINK files yet, but we do have ts_vcf() and ts_eigenstrat() conversion functions (see this exercise from our workshop for a quick overview). You can use these functions to produce outputs from your simulations converted from the original tree sequence, then do the necessary PLINK conversion to be able to run ADMIXTURE or STRUCTURE.
crumbs: 16  PCA, STRUCTURE, LAI, DATES, IBD

title: PCA, STRUCTURE, LAI, DATES, IBD
text:
PCA
PCA is an incredibly popular method in population genetics, but there’s been quite a bit of controversy surrounding it, with a highly combative paper criticizing the application of PCA in all of population genetics, almost to a point of claiming that none of the published results can be really trusted.
As an example, take a look at Figure 5 in the paper, demonstrating that an Indian population can be arbitrarily placed in proximity to Europeans, East Asians, and Africans, simply by tweaking the sample sizes of all groups before they applying PCA on their genotype data.
If you’re curious about this issue, you have now all the tools at your disposal to be able to use slendr to evaluate patterns and (un)expected behavior of PCA in the light of the criticisms in the paper.
Things you could take a look into are:

How do imbalanced sample sizes from different populations distort the shape of a PCA compared to equal sample sizes?
How does access to ancient DNA samples (or lack of ancient DNA samples) affect the signal of admixture in a PCA? What other demographic factors could lead us to false ideas about admixture in a PCA?
Under which conditions does projection of ancient DNA samples on a PCA based on modern DNA reference panel lead to misleading results?
How is a phylogenetic tree structure in general reflected in a shape of PCA?

If you’d like an inspiration, you can take a look at a work-in-progress chapter about simulating PCA (but beware that it’s still unfinished and not proofread!). I suggest working with the convenient PCA R package smartsnp.
crumbs: 16  PCA, STRUCTURE, LAI, DATES, IBD

title: PCA, STRUCTURE, LAI, DATES, IBD
section: Local ancestry inference (LAI), DATES dating, and IBD segments
text:
Local ancestry inference (LAI), DATES dating, and IBD segments
In the chapter on simulating haplotypes you’ve learned about the slendr functions ts_tracts() and ts_ibd(), which make it possible to obtain perfect, exact, truth about admixture tracts and haplotype sharing from customized simulations.
You’ve also learned how easy it is to generate VCF files from these simulations. This opens up the possibility to generate genomic data from all sorts of models relevant for your research questions and use them for all sorts of applications briefly summarized in points 1.-3. at the beginning of this chapter.
If you have software for LAI (such as MOSAIC, FLARE, RFMix, etc.), admixture dating (DATES), or IBD inference (IBDSeq, IBIS, AncIBD), it’s now very easy for you to connect simulations with this kind of external software—the sky is the limit!

title: Appendix A — Installation instructions
text:
Installation steps
The chapters of this book focused on population genomics and simulations rely pretty much exclusively on the R package slendr, plus an assortment of other useful R packages for data science (most of which will be automatically installed alongside slendr). Below are instructions how to prepare everything that will be needed before the start of our workshop.
Please don’t hesitate to get in touch with me over email at contact [snail sign] bodkan.net if you run into any problems with this setup procedure or anything else related to this! If you’re reading this in preparation for one of my in-person workshops, you can also catch me whenever you see me at the teaching venue.
install.packages("slendr")
Note: If you get an error during the installation, please copy-and-paste the entire output from this command and send it to me via email.
library(slendr)
init_env(uv = TRUE)

pop <- population("pop", time = 1, N = 1000)
model <- compile_model(list(pop), generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000)
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)

text:
I assume you already have R and RStudio installed on your computer (any reasonably recent version will do).
Open RStudio and copy this into the R console to install the slendr package:




Paste this little testing simulation script into the R console to make sure that everything works correctly.

First, go to Session -> Restart R in the RStudio menu.
Then paste this command into the R console:

slendr::setup_env(agree = TRUE)

When the command finishes running, copy-paste the following version of the above-mentioned testing script into the R console (note that the uv = TRUE is missing in the init_env() function — I’m happy to explain during the workshop).

title: Appendix A — Installation instructions
text:
Optional
The following isn’t something you need to do before the start of the workshop. It’s something we can deal with towards the end of the workshop (if it even becomes necessary).

Running heavy slendr simulations
If you decide you’d like to run some really big simulations (perhaps during the open-ended sessions at the end of the workshop) it might be necessary to run your models on a bigger computing server. I suspect you have some remote computing facilities available for doing heavy bioinformatics work, etc.
If that’s the case, you’ll want to also install and setup slendr and the R packages mentioned above on this remote server as well. Just repeat the same instructions and you should be good to go.


Running third-party software
Similarly, in the open-ended workshop sessions, you will have the opportunity to apply the modeling techniques learned throughout the exercises in a practical context of your own research. As you work on the exercises, you might get an inspiration for applying this or that technique to study a particular aspect of your research question, which might involve third-party software such as qpAdm, IBDSeq, DATES, ADMIXTURE/STRUCTURE etc. If that ends up being the case, I suggest you try to install slendr on the (again, probably remote?) computer you normally use to do your research.
